title: Outsourcing Memory to External Tools: A Review of ‘Intention Offloading’
authors: Sam J. Gilbert; Annika Boldt; Chhavi Sachdeva; Chiara Scarampi; Pei‐Chun Tsai
design: Narrative review synthesising multiple experimental/behavioural, developmental, ageing, and fMRI studies of intention offloading; not a single primary study
n: not reported in retrieved text (pooled synthesis of multiple studies, each with own N; no aggregate k or total N given in supplied text)
population: Multiple populations across cited studies: adults (younger 18–30 years and older 65–84 years, e.g. Scarampi & Gilbert), children aged approximately 7–13 years (Redshaw et al.) and children as young as 4 years (Bulley et al.) — mixed ages incl. minors across the body of reviewed work; individual study settings not consistently specified (mostly laboratory/online experiments)
ai_exposure: Not an AI tool review; exposure is to non-AI external memory aids/cognitive tools within lab tasks — e.g. self-set 'reminders' in computerised drag-and-drop tasks (Gilbert paradigm), optional vs. forced reminder-setting, vs. relying on internal/unaided memory, contrasted with real-world external tools such as diaries, calendars, sticky notes, and smartphone/wearable alerts mentioned as everyday examples
measures: Delayed intention/prospective memory performance via a computerised drag-and-circle intention offloading task (Gilbert paradigm); rate/proportion of reminder-setting; accuracy under forced internal-memory vs. forced-reminder trials; optimal reminders paradigm comparing actual vs. optimal choice behaviour; metacognitive confidence/prediction ratings; naturalistic prospective memory task (collecting web-link bonuses at 2, 5, 7 days); fMRI multivariate pattern analysis of brain activity during metacognitive monitoring/control and during intention maintenance (lateral and medial rostral prefrontal cortex)
key_finding: Across the reviewed studies, individuals systematically set more external reminders than would be optimal (a positive reminder bias), and this offloading behaviour is triggered in part by metacognitive beliefs about one's own memory ability (independent of objective ability), by a preference to avoid cognitive effort, and by strategy perseveration from prior experience; reminders themselves are highly effective at reducing forgetting; children under ~9 do not yet translate metacognitive knowledge of forgetting risk into strategic reminder-setting whereas older children and adults do; older adults do not fully compensate for memory impairment even when free to set reminders and tend to be overconfident, unlike younger adults who are underconfident and over-rely on reminders; neurally, intention offloading is associated with a metacognitive process (cross-classifiable monitoring/control signals) and has dissociable effects on lateral versus medial rostral prefrontal cortex activity. The authors frame these as associations/behavioural patterns, not causal claims about long-term cognitive harm or benefit from tool use.
effect_size: Gilbert et al.: forgetting rate "about 45%" using own memory vs "only around 5%" using external reminders. Gilbert (Experiment 1a): metacognitive evaluations predicted reminder use even when "entirely unrelated to objective accuracy (r = -0.01)". Text states the correlation between offloading-task performance and naturalistic bonus-collection task was "numerically small but statistically highly significant" (no exact r/p given). Internal-memory accuracy in optimal reminders paradigm typically "around 50–60%"; reminder accuracy typically "90–100%". No other point estimates, CIs, or p-values are given in the supplied text.
limitations: Authors note: "the studies reviewed above were mostly conducted with rather artificial experimental tasks"; "we do not yet know much about how individuals' cognitive offloading strategies, measured in the laboratory, relate to their use of cognitive offloading in everyday life"; findings on ageing/development are cross-sectional and the authors state "this conclusion would be stronger... if it were supported by longitudinal rather than cross-sectional evidence"; effects of metacognitive interventions on cognitive offloading "have been inconsistent" between studies; "the cross-domain organisation of metacognition and cognitive offloading is still poorly understood"; results on domain-general vs domain-specific offloading are described as "inconsistent" across studies (Ball et al. vs Meyerhoff et al.).
caveat_flags: non-adult sample (in some cited studies); cross-sectional; narrative review not systematic/meta-analytic pooling; artificial/laboratory tasks noted by authors as limitation; inconsistent findings across cited studies; no single aggregate N or k reported; some findings from studies described as 'in preparation'

title: Conversational AI Powered by Large Language Models Amplifies False Memories in Witness Interviews
authors: Samantha Chan; Pat Pataranutaporn; Aditya Suri; Wazeer Zulfikar; Pattie Maes; Elizabeth F. Loftus
design: preregistered between-subjects RCT, 4 arms (control, survey, pre-scripted chatbot, generative chatbot), 2-phase (immediate + 1-week follow-up)
n: N=200 participants Phase 1 (50 per condition); Phase 2 N=194 (control 49, survey 48, pre-scripted 48, generative 49); 39 additional participants excluded for failing attention checks in Phase 1 survey
population: Recruited via Prolific online recruitment platform; prescreened to be fluent in English and aged 18 and above; adults; country not reported in retrieved text beyond "online pool"
ai_exposure: Four conditions after watching a crime video: (1) Control - no false-memory-inducing interaction; (2) Survey-based - 25 yes/no questions (5 misleading) via Google Forms; (3) Pre-scripted Chatbot - conversational agent asking same questions with no adaptive feedback; (4) Generative Chatbot - GPT-4-powered conversational agent that gave LLM-generated feedback agreeing with and reinforcing participant answers, including misinformation, on the 5 critical misleading questions
measures: Number of false memories induced (count of critical misleading questions answered >4 on 7-point Definitely No–Definitely Yes follow-up scale) measured immediately and after 1 week; confidence in false memories (0–3 scale derived from follow-up scale) measured immediately and after 1 week; confidence in true memories (non-critical questions); emotional state via Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM) scale; cognitive workload via Raw NASA-TLX; moderating factors (AI/chatbot familiarity, interest in crime investigations, age, gender, education, AI attitude, need for cognition) via questionnaire and mixed-effects regression
key_finding: The generative chatbot condition significantly induced more immediate false memories than control, survey, and pre-scripted chatbot conditions, inducing over 3 times more immediate false memories than control and 1.7 times more than the survey method; 36.4% of users' responses to the generative chatbot were misled. After one week, false memories induced by the generative chatbot remained constant (unlike control and survey conditions which significantly increased), and confidence in these false memories remained higher than control after one week. Users less familiar with chatbots but more familiar with AI technology, and more interested in crime investigations, were significantly more susceptible to forming immediate false memories. All associations are correlational/moderational as framed by the authors, though causal experimental manipulation (random assignment to condition) is used for condition effects.
effect_size: Immediate false memories: Kruskal-Wallis χ2 = 32.468, P = 4.170e-07; means: control M=0.54, s.d.=0.877, pct=10.8%; survey M=1.08, s.d.=0.821, pct=21.6%; pre-scripted M=1.34, s.d.=1.28, pct=26.8%; generative M=1.82, s.d.=1.24, pct=36.4%. Posthoc Dunn (FDR): generative vs survey P=0.0115; generative vs pre-scripted P=0.0395; control vs survey P=0.00585; control vs pre-scripted P=0.00135; control vs generative P<0.0001. Confidence in immediate false memories: Kruskal-Wallis χ2=17.230, P=0.000634; generative M=1.02, s.d.=0.699, P=0.000338 vs control; pre-scripted M=0.811, s.d.=0.749, P=0.0236; survey M=0.838, s.d.=0.689, P=0.0100; control M=0.475, s.d.=0.738. 1-week persistence: Wilcoxon generative P=0.950 (immediate M=1.82, s.d.=1.24; 1wk M=1.84, s.d.=1.18); pre-scripted P=0.489; control P=0.00261 (immediate M=0.54; 1wk M=1.02); survey P=0.0105 (immediate M=1.08; 1wk M=1.46). 1-week confidence: generative M=1.12, s.d.=0.727 vs control M=0.684, s.d.=0.782, P=0.00424; generative vs pre-scripted M=0.792, s.d.=0.726, P=0.0336. Mixed-effects model: Experience with AI, Estimate=0.55894, Z=3.283, P=0.001025**; Experience with Chatbot, Estimate=-0.64943, Z=-3.582, P=0.000341***; Interest in crime scenes, Estimate=0.22501, Z=2.524, P=0.011587*.
limitations: Future research could explore the boundaries of selective memory manipulation with more complex or interconnected memories; longitudinal studies examining persistence of AI-induced false memories beyond one week would provide valuable insights into durability of effects; the study notes prior AI familiarity vs chatbot-specific familiarity distinction may confound interpretation of moderating factors.
caveat_flags: preprint; self-report only; single site (Prolific online sample); no delayed retention test beyond one week; outcome is proxy not learning

title: Not all cognitive offloading is equal: distinguishing dependent and autonomous offloading to generative AI
authors: Qiuhan Zhu; Xiangnan Li; Yiang Dong; Pengcheng Chang; Mengmeng Fan
design: three-wave time-lagged survey study (T1, T2, T3, each 2 weeks apart); not stated as preregistered
n: Final analytic sample N=589 (of 742 at T1; 672 completed T2; 631 completed T3); subgroup: students n=516, early-career workers n=73
population: Recruited from universities and young professional communities via online survey platforms; primarily Chinese university students and early-career workers; M age=23.69, SD=3.24; 51.1% female; inclusion criteria required aged 18 or above; undergraduate (54.3%), master's (25.3%), doctoral (8.0%) students, and young professionals (12.4%); adults
ai_exposure: Generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, ERNIE Bot, Kimi, Doubao) used for learning or work-related cognitive tasks over ≥3 months; not an experimental manipulation but a survey-measured distinction between two self-reported modes of AI engagement: "dependent cognitive offloading" (delegating core thinking to AI, accepting AI-generated answers with minimal evaluation) vs. "autonomous cognitive offloading" (using AI as a scaffold, retaining cognitive agency)
measures: T1: Dependent cognitive offloading (4 items, α=0.773), Autonomous cognitive offloading (4 items, α=0.767), Metacognitive monitoring (adapted from metacognitive awareness inventory, 4 items, α=0.765), Task complexity (4 items, α=0.760). T2: Cognitive agency transfer (novel scale, 4 items, α=0.773), Intrinsic motivation (adapted scale, 4 items, α=0.837), Immediate benefit (4 items, α=0.750). T3: Subsequent autonomous capability (4 items, α=0.793), Creativity (4 items, α=0.747), Deep processing (4 items, α=0.848), Independent judgment (4 items, α=0.746). All self-report, 5-point Likert scales.
key_finding: Dependent and autonomous cognitive offloading are distinct, only weakly correlated dimensions (r=0.08) with divergent downstream correlates: dependent offloading was positively associated with cognitive agency transfer and negatively associated with intrinsic motivation, while autonomous offloading was unrelated to cognitive agency transfer but positively associated with intrinsic motivation. Cognitive agency transfer was negatively associated with all four T3 cognitive outcomes, and intrinsic motivation was positively associated with all four. Metacognitive monitoring attenuated (but did not eliminate) the dependent-offloading-to-agency-transfer association but did not buffer the negative motivational association. Both offloading modes showed comparable associations with immediate benefit despite opposite downstream correlates. Authors explicitly frame this as correlational/associational evidence, not causal, and outcomes as self-reported/perceived rather than performance-based.
effect_size: Dep. offloading–CAT: r=0.38, p<0.001; β=0.35 (b=0.35, SE=0.04, p<0.001). Aut. offloading–CAT: r=-0.01, p=0.83; β=-0.05 (b=-0.05, SE=0.04, p=0.18). Dep. offloading–IM: r=-0.19, p<0.001; β=-0.23 (b=-0.25, SE=0.04, p<0.001). Aut. offloading–IM: r=0.29, p<0.001; β=0.28 (b=0.30, SE=0.04, p<0.001). CAT→outcomes β range -0.15 to -0.29 (all p<0.001); IM→outcomes β range 0.26 to 0.36 (all p<0.001). Indirect effects (bootstrapped, 95% CI): Dep. offloading via CAT on outcomes β=-0.05 to -0.10 (CIs excluding zero); via IM β=-0.06 to -0.09; Aut. offloading via IM β=0.07 to 0.10 (CIs excluding zero); via CAT all CIs included zero. Moderation: interaction dep. offloading × metacog monitoring on CAT b=-0.14, SE=0.04, p<0.001; simple slopes: low monitoring β=0.48 (p<0.001), high monitoring β=0.21 (p<0.001). Interaction on IM: b=0.01, SE=0.04, p=0.72 (ns); slopes low=-0.19 (p<0.001), high=-0.17 (p<0.001). Immediate benefit correlations: r=0.22 with both dep. and aut. offloading (both p<0.001); with subsequent autonomous capability r=0.06, p=0.14; with independent judgment r=-0.00, p=0.91. Correlation between dep. and aut. offloading: r=0.08, p=0.049. CFA fit: χ2(847)=1825.22, CFI=0.92, TLI=0.91, RMSEA=0.044, SRMR=0.042. Structural model fit: χ2(52)=138.47, CFI=0.96, TLI=0.93, RMSEA=0.053, SRMR=0.038. Latent SEM fit: χ2(891)=938.85, CFI=0.99, TLI=0.99, RMSEA=0.010.
limitations: All outcomes were self-reported, not performance-based measures, so findings speak to perceived/subjective cognitive functioning, not demonstrated ability; common method variance is a concern for newly developed scales (though mitigated by temporal separation and poor fit of single-factor model, CFI=0.51); three-wave design supports tests of indirect associations but does not establish mediation in the causal sense—no baseline (T1) measures of mediators/outcomes, so cannot rule out reverse or reciprocal influence or stable third variables; bootstrapped "indirect effects" should be read as indirect associations consistent with, not confirmatory of, hypothesized pathways; causal inference requires baseline-controlled designs (e.g., RI-CLPM) and experimental manipulation, which was not undertaken; core mechanisms incompletely measured (need-satisfaction not measured, only intrinsic motivation as proximal consequence; cognitive agency transfer measured as single-occasion state rather than repeated process); new constructs not tested for discriminant validity against measured instruments of adjacent constructs (AI dependency, automation complacency, blind trust, critical AI literacy, self-regulated learning); sample comprised primarily Chinese university students and early-career workers, worker subsample small (n=73); participants reported on AI use across heterogeneous tasks rather than a single standardized task, increasing ecological validity but leaving open which kinds of offloading drive associations; did not directly test whether users can or cannot detect maladaptive AI use.
caveat_flags: self-report only; cross-sectional-like limitations despite multi-wave design (no baseline mediator/outcome measures); no delayed retention test; outcome is proxy not learning; single country/culture sample; small subsample (workers n=73); newly developed unvalidated scales; common method variance risk; authors explicitly caution against causal interpretation

title: Borrowed or kept? How self-generation-first and direct-adoption AI workflows shape immediate unaided reasoning
authors: Chenghai Liu; Jiayao Guo; Rongxia Gao; Xiangnan Chen; Qiuhan Zhu; Pengcheng Chang
design: preregistered three-arm randomized experiment (self-generation-first, direct-adoption, no-AI), unaided transfer task 15–20 min later
n: 900 randomized participants; primary analysis sample N = 659 (autonomous = 222, dependent = 225, no-AI = 212); per-protocol n = 585 (172/201/212... note text gives per-protocol …
population: not reported in retrieved text (no country/setting/age specified beyond 'participants'; adult status not reported in retrieved text)
ai_exposure: essay writing under one of: self-generation-first autonomous AI workflow (commit own position, then interrogate AI), direct-adoption dependent AI workflow, or no AI
measures: Behavioral: process log measures (outline submission, proportion of AI suggestions adopted vs. rewritten, number of AI calls, time on task) used for manipulation fidelity checks. Self-report: trait/process measures — ACO subscale (DACOS), Reflective Thinking Questionnaire, Critical Thinking Disposition Inventory, state metacognitive-monitoring scale, Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (interest/effort subscales), AI-use frequency item. Behavioral/rated-performance (blind human rating, not self-report or physiological): the three objective outcomes — reasoning quality, idea diversity, originality — each scored 1–7 by two blind raters using a rubric (this is the primary outcome measure type). No physiological measures reported.
key_finding: On the unaided task, dependent users reasoned worse than never-used-AI participants, whereas autonomous users did not fall below that baseline; authors frame this as an immediate near-transfer decrement rather than demonstrated lasting de-skilling
effect_size: dependent users scored below participants who had never used AI [adjusted difference = −0.38, 95% CI [−0.59, −0.18], d = −0.28, two-sided p = 0.0002, FDR q = 0.0006]. limitations: authors state the design cannot exclude a metacognitive pathway; the estimate belongs to the workflow contrast as a whole rather than to any single component (self-generation, elaboration, revision, effort, autonomy are confounded); a generation-effect account is consistent but cannot be weighed against alternatives; no mechanism is established; result is immediate near-transfer decrement, not demonstrated lasting de-skilling
caveat_flags: outcome is proxy not learning (near-transfer task, not real-world skill); mechanism not established; short-term outcome only (15-20 min), no long-term follow-up; attrition from 900 randomized to 659 analyzed

title: ChatGPT-generated help produces learning gains equivalent to human tutor-authored help on mathematics skills
authors: Zachary A. Pardos; Shreya Bhandari
design: Randomised controlled experiment, 3x4 design (3 hint conditions x 4 subjects), online, random assignment via Qualtrics; not stated as preregistered
n: Total N = 274 participants after exclusions (Control n=90, human-tutor hints n=86, ChatGPT hints n=98); recruited 394, 120 excluded. RQ1 hint-quality analysis unit: 75 problems (questions) ChatGPT was prompted to generate hints for, rated by 6 undergraduate raters
population: Mechanical Turk workers (US-based crowdsourcing platform, online); adults — required at least a high school degree and MTurk "Master" designation; median age group of participants was 36-40
ai_exposure: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5, "Dec 15 Version") used to generate worked-solution hints for algebra/statistics problems; compared against human tutor-authored hints (from OATutor, authored by UC Berkeley undergraduates with tutoring experience) and a no-hint control condition (correctness feedback + bottom-out hint only)
measures: Learning gain measured via a three-item pre-test and identical three-item post-test per subject (algebra/statistics problems from OpenStax textbooks); also measured session/time-on-task; hint quality measured via 3-point quality check (correct answer, correct work, no inappropriate language) rated by 6 undergraduate raters with Fleiss' Kappa for inter-rater reliability
key_finding: ChatGPT-generated hints produced statistically significant learning gains (17%) compared to the no-hint control (1.85%), while human tutor-authored hints (11.62%) were not statistically significantly different from control. ChatGPT hints produced higher learning gains than human tutor hints in all subjects, but the ChatGPT and human-authored hint learning gains were not statistically significantly separable. No significant interaction between condition and subject. ChatGPT hints contained incorrect work/answer in 32% of cases (disqualification rate), reducible to near 0% for algebra subjects and 13% for statistics via self-consistency mitigation.
effect_size: ChatGPT: pre-test 43.51%, post-test 60.52%, learning gain 17.00%, p«0.001. Human tutor: pre-test 53.46%, post-test 65.09%, gain 11.62%, p=0.001. Control: pre-test 55.15%, post-test 57.01%, gain 1.85%, p=0.192. Two-Way ANOVA on ranked data: condition F(2,262)=5.037, p=0.0071; subject F(3,262)=6.737, p=0.0002; interaction F(6,262)=0.901, p=0.495. Dunn's post-hoc: ChatGPT vs control p=0.011; human tutor vs control p=0.087; ChatGPT vs human tutor p=0.416. Session time: hint conditions vs control p«0.001; ChatGPT vs human tutor p=0.614. Power analysis (assumed Cohen's d=0.5, alpha=0.05): 0.910 (control vs human-tutor), 0.926 (control vs ChatGPT), 0.920 (human-tutor vs ChatGPT). Hint quality: Fleiss' Kappa 0.929 (Elementary Algebra), 0.864 (Intermediate Algebra), 0.857 (College Algebra), 0.916 (Statistics). Of 75 problems, average 24 disqualified (32%); Elementary Algebra 25%, Intermediate Algebra 47% (highest), College Algebra 27%, Statistics 29%. Self-consistency error rates: Elementary Algebra 0%, Intermediate Algebra 2%, College Algebra 2%, Statistics 13%. Median word count: ChatGPT hints 355 (min 142, max 669); human hints 277 (min 79, max 667).
limitations: Hints could only be produced for problems without graphical figures due to ChatGPT's text-only input/output limitation at the time; study relied on a closed-source LLM whose model weights are not public; used crowdsourced (Mechanical Turk) learners rather than in-situ secondary/post-secondary students, though authors cite findings that crowdsourced results agree with in-situ learners; high attrition rate of 30%, though fairly even across conditions; scope limited to secondary and early post-secondary mathematics.
caveat_flags: no delayed retention test; outcome is proxy not learning (3-item pre/post test); crowdsourced sample not classroom students; closed-source LLM (model weights not public); high attrition (30%); self-report age range only; single platform (Mechanical Turk); not stated as preregistered

title: AI Meets the Classroom: When Do Large Language Models Harm Learning?
authors: Matthias Lehmann; Philipp B. Cornelius; Fabian J. Sting
design: Field study (Study 1, two-way FE and FE2SLS panel analysis) + two pre-registered, incentivized, randomized between-subjects lab experiments (Studies 2 and 3), each with pre-test/learning-phase/post-test; exploratory pooled analyses combining Studies 2 and 3
n: Study 1: N=113 students (56 IS course, 57 BA course), unit of analysis student–question, 6,775 student–question observations total (6,594 used in main models). Study 2: 108 subjects recruited, 107 analyzed (54 vs 53 approx. per control/treatment, exact split not stated). Study 3: 72 enrolled, 69 analyzed after exclusions. Combined exploratory sample (Studies 2+3 treated/all subjects): up to 176 observations in heterogeneous-effects and perceived-learning regressions; 94 observations in usage-behavior regressions (treated subjects only).
population: Study 1: graduate students in two programming courses (information systems and business analytics) at a public Dutch university, adults (graduate students), age not otherwise reported. Studies 2 and 3: subjects recruited from a laboratory participant pool at a public German university, described as "enrolled students," adults (age discretized into buckets in survey, e.g. mean age bucket ~2.4-2.8 on a 1-5 scale; exact ages not reported in retrieved text). All settings university/lab-based, adults.
ai_exposure: ChatGPT (OpenAI). Study 1: proxy measure of ChatGPT use via similarity between student code submissions and ChatGPT-generated code (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613), no explicit condition assignment (observational/quasi-experimental using ChatGPT outages as instrument). Studies 2 and 3: randomized access to ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125) via API chat window during the learning phase only (not pre/post-test) vs. control condition with no LLM access; Study 3 identical to Study 2 but with copy-and-paste enabled for both conditions (Study 2 had copy-paste unintentionally disabled).
measures: Learning outcomes decomposed into: (1) overall learning outcome = Post-test score (number of correct answers out of 20 programming questions, administered before and after learning phase); (2) topic volume = number of correctly answered practice questions during the 45-minute Learning Phase (24 parts); (3) topic understanding = residual effect on Post-test after controlling for Learning Phase progress. Also: Perceived Learning (five-point Likert self-report scale) controlling for actual Post-test−Pre-test difference. Study 1: coding assignment Grade (normalized 0-1) per question, ChatGPT Similarity and Cumulative ChatGPT Similarity (Damerau-Levenshtein similarity to ChatGPT-generated solutions) as proxy for substitutive LLM use, with ChatGPT service outages used as an instrument.
key_finding: Across two pre-registered, incentivized lab experiments, the authors find "no significant effect of LLM access on overall learning outcomes." In exploratory analyses, effects depend on usage behavior: students who use LLMs to substitute learning activities (asking for solutions) increase topic volume but decrease topic understanding; students who use LLMs to complement learning (asking for explanations) increase understanding without increasing volume. In the field study (Study 1), using ChatGPT to generate solutions is associated with a higher grade on the current question but a lower grade on subsequent questions (interpreted as a negative effect of substitutive LLM use on learning), robust to an instrumental-variable approach using ChatGPT outages, though the immediate-grade benefit becomes non-significant under IV. LLM access also increases perceived learning beyond what is explained by actual learning gains, and widens the gap between low- and high-prior-knowledge students (heterogeneous treatment effects), with the authors stating "LLMs appear to increase inequality in education."
effect_size: Study 1 FE: ChatGPT Similarity effect on Grade = 0.18*** (SE 0.05); Cum. ChatGPT Similarity = -0.02*** (SE 0.00); F-statistic 7.64***; R2=0.29. Study 1 FE2SLS: ChatGPT Similarity effect on Grade = -0.35 (SE 0.56, p=0.334, not significant); Cum. ChatGPT Similarity = -0.06*** (SE 0.02, p=0.002). First stage: ChatGPT Outages p=0.005; Cum. ChatGPT Outages p=0.002. Study 2: Post-test control=7.9(4.2), treatment=9.0(4.7); Welch's t-tests p=0.425 (pre-test), p=0.175 (learning phase), p=0.206 (post-test), p=0.376 (post-pre difference); regression treatment effect on Post-test p=0.580, on understanding p=0.562, on volume p=0.214. Study 3: Pre-test p=0.157; Learning Phase treated +4 questions p=0.003; Post-test +2 questions p=0.092; Post-pre diff p=0.312; regression: overall learning p=0.298, understanding p=0.359, volume 2.614** (SE 1.020) p=0.013. Exploratory copy/paste effect on Post-test: -0.249 (0.737) p=0.737; on understanding -1.407*** (0.525) p=0.009; on volume 1.733** (0.800) p=0.033. Solutions effect on Post-test: -0.312*** (0.066); Explanations effect: 0.249** (0.125) p=0.05. Heterogeneous effects: Treatment×Pre-test>Median on Post-test 2.528** (1.142) p=0.028; on understanding 1.613** (0.754) p=0.034; low prior-knowledge treated understood significantly less than control (p=0.043). Perceived Learning: Treatment effect 0.338** (0.166) p=0.044, and 0.348** (0.170) p=0.043 in second model.
limitations: Authors state: exploratory findings "should ideally be replicated in controlled experiments and with additional field data." They "abstract away from the neurological building blocks of understanding, such as conceptual and factual understanding... and memory." Study 1 relies on a proxy measure (ChatGPT Similarity) since actual LLM use could not be directly observed ("Since we cannot directly observe whether a student used ChatGPT, ChatGPT Similarity is a proxy for this behavior"). Study 2 had an unintended methodological issue (copy-and-paste disabled), which the authors note affected LLM usage and necessitated Study 3 and revised hypotheses. Authors also note that the effect of LLMs on workplace learning was not studied and may generalize differently, and that further research is needed on how task complexity and LLM usage patterns affect workplace learning-by-doing.
caveat_flags: preprint; outcome is proxy not learning; self-report only (perceived learning measure); exploratory/non-preregistered analyses for usage-behavior and heterogeneity results; single institution per study; no delayed retention test; small subgroup exclusions; unintended confound in Study 2 (copy-paste disabled); supplied text capped at 90,000 characters; later sections may be absent; mixed evidence base: Study 1 is an observational panel field study; Studies 2-3 are preregistered randomised lab experiments

title: Large language models improve clinical decision making of medical students through patient simulation and structured feedback: a randomized controlled trial
authors: Emilia Brügge; Sarah Ricchizzi; Malin Arenbeck; Marius Niklas Keller; Lina Schur; Walter Stummer; Markus Holling; Max Hao Lu; Dogus Darici
design: Two-group randomized controlled trial (closed-label, participants blinded); repeated measures over 4 scenarios; not stated as preregistered
n: Total N=21 analyzed (24 randomized, 29 initially agreed, 5 dropped before randomization, 3 excluded post-randomization for technical/data issues); feedback group n=10, control group n=11
population: Medical students at the University of Münster, Germany, recruited Nov 2023–Feb 2024; ages 19–35 (adults); none had clinical rotations, half had no prior knowledge
ai_exposure: OpenAI's ChatGPT 3.5 (free version) via Playground interface simulating patients (herniated lumbar disc, stroke, meningitis, concussion/TBI); control group had AI-simulated patient conversation only; feedback group had the same conversation plus ChatGPT-generated feedback (CRI-HTI-based ratings and three improvement suggestions) after each of four scenarios
measures: Clinical decision-making/clinical reasoning assessed via the Clinical Reasoning Indicator-History Taking Inventory (CRI-HTI), an 8-item, 5-point Likert scale across three competence domains (Focusing questions, Creating context, Securing information), rated by two blinded independent human raters from chat transcripts (ICC=0.924); also a post-training survey on perceived realism, authenticity, accuracy, and feasibility of the simulation
key_finding: The feedback group showed significantly better CDM outcomes than the control group, with steady improvement from scenario 1 to scenario 4; improvements were significant in the subdomains "creating context" and "securing information," but not in "focusing questions" (attributed to a possible ceiling effect); participants in both groups rated the simulations as highly accurate, feasible, and realistic; authors state the results "indicate that AI-based medical history conversations with feedback can simulate conducive teaching and learning scenarios, and improve students' CDM performances."
effect_size: Feedback group M=3.604 ± 0.130 (95% CI: 3.331, 3.878) vs control group M=3.017 ± 0.118 (95% CI: 2.770, 3.264); F(1,20)=4.436, p=.049, partial η2=0.198 (strong effect); creating context p=.046; securing information p=.018; focusing questions p=.265; baseline word count t(18)=0.219, p=.829; ICC=0.924; sociodemographic comparisons: age χ2(6)=7.58, p=.271; gender χ2(1)=0.095, p=.757; prior knowledge χ2(3)=0.649, p=.885; semester χ2(3)=3.560, p=.313; survey ratings: accuracy M=8.67/10 ± 2.01, feasibility M=8.38/10 ± 1.88, realism M=7.81/10 ± 1.40
limitations: ChatGPT 3.5's training data only extends to January 2022; ongoing model updates (e.g., March 2023 update) may affect reproducibility and it has not been tested whether results replicate with newer versions; conversations were conducted in German, and answers/feedback may be more precise in English since ChatGPT was originally trained on English texts; the sample is relatively small though a significant effect was found, and future studies should increase statistical power and participant numbers and examine effects across different geographic/cultural audiences; some participants learned to combine multiple questions into one prompt to overcome ChatGPT's latency, which does not reflect realistic medical history conversation behavior, so use of ChatGPT may not reflect how participants would actually engage in real life.
caveat_flags: N<30; single site; self-report component for realism/feasibility ratings; outcome is proxy not learning; no delayed retention test; small sample size acknowledged by authors; language/translation limitation (German vs English); model version reproducibility limitation; unrepresentative prompting behavior (combined questions) noted as limitation

title: Cognitive ease at a cost: LLMs reduce mental effort but compromise depth in student scientific inquiry
authors: Matthias Stadler; Maria Bannert; Michael Sailer
design: randomised between-subjects experiment, 2 arms (ChatGPT3.5 vs Google)
n: 91 students (Web search n = 47; LLM n = 44); note: 92 recruited, 1 excluded for not following instructions
population: university students; country/setting not reported in retrieved text; adults implied by 'university students' but not explicitly stated in retrieved text
ai_exposure: ChatGPT3.5 used for information gathering on the socio-scientific issue of nanoparticles in sunscreen, compared to traditional Google search
measures: Cognitive load (ICL, ECL, GCL): self-report (7-item Likert questionnaire, 1-7 agreement, Klepsch et al. 2017). Quality of justifications and recommendation direction: behavioral/performance (coded from participants' written text by two independent raters, k=0.92 and k=0.89 respectively). Prior domain knowledge: behavioral/performance (8-item multiple-choice knowledge test, adapted PKNT).
key_finding: Students using LLMs experienced significantly lower cognitive load but demonstrated lower-quality reasoning and argumentation in their final recommendations compared to those using traditional search engines; homogeneity of recommendations/justifications did not differ significantly between groups
effect_size: ANCOVAs controlling for prior knowledge (Table 2): H1.1 – ECL: MWeb=3.96 (SD 1.55), MLLM=3.00 (SD 1.67), F=8.26, p=0.005, η2=0.09. H1.2 – ICL: MWeb=4.43 (SD 1.60), MLLM=3.16 (SD 1.46), F=16.48, p<0.001, η2=0.15. H1.3 – GCL: MWeb=4.79 (SD 1.18), MLLM=3.14 (SD 1.53), F=33.06, p<0.001, η2=0.27. H2 – Quality of justifications: MWeb=1.87 (SD 1.10), MLLM=1.20 (SD 0.77), F=11.18, p=0.001, η2=0.11 ('Students in the web search condition listed significantly more relevant arguments in their statements than students in the LLM condition'). Exploratory mediation via GCL: significant indirect effect (β = 0.15; p = 0.020) and no significant direct effect (β = 0.19; p = 0.095), 'indicating a full mediation.' H3 (homogeneity of recommendations, not supported): χ2(2) = 1.78; p = 0.411.
limitations: not reported in retrieved text
caveat_flags: single task/topic (nanoparticles in sunscreen); small, imbalanced arms (Web search 47 / LLM 44)

title: Beware of metacognitive laziness: Effects of generative artificial intelligence on learning motivation, processes, and performance
authors: Yizhou Fan; Luzhen Tang; Huixiao Le; Kejie Shen; Shufang Tan; Yueying Zhao; Yüan Shen; Xinyu Li; Dragan Gašević
design: randomised experimental study, lab setting, 4 groups (ChatGPT, human expert, writing analytics tools, no extra tool)
n: 117 university students total (CN group, 30 participants; AI group, 35 participants; HE group, 25 participants; CL group, 27 participants)
population: university students; country/setting not reported in retrieved text; adult status not reported in retrieved text
ai_exposure: ChatGPT support during a writing task, compared to chat with a human expert, writing analytics tools, or no extra tool
measures: Essay score improvement and knowledge/transfer test scores: behavioral (task performance/test performance, scored by researchers or via choice-question tests); Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI - interest/enjoyment, perceived competence, effort/importance, pressure/tension): self-report; SRL process frequency and sequence (from learning trace data - navigational logs, click streams, mouse movement, keyboard strokes, parsed via trace parser and process mining/FOMM): behavioral (trace-data derived)
key_finding: Learners across support groups showed no difference in post-task intrinsic motivation; there were significant differences in the frequency and sequences of self-regulated learning processes among groups; the ChatGPT group outperformed others in essay score improvement, but their knowledge gain and transfer were not significantly different, and the authors note ChatGPT may promote dependence on technology and trigger 'metacognitive laziness'.
effect_size: "The ANOVA results indicated no significant differences in essay scores (F=1.275, p=0.286, η2=0.033) before revision, but significant differences in score improvements (F=4.549, p=0.005, η2=0.108) after revision... the AI group showed a higher score improvement than the CN group (mean difference = 1.970, p-adjusted = 0.037), the HE group (mean difference = 2.120, p-adjusted = 0.025), and the CL group (mean difference = 2.200, p-adjusted = 0.012)." Pairwise table: CL-AI mean difference -2.200, 95% CI (-4.033, -0.367), p-adjusted=0.012; CN-AI mean difference -1.970, 95% CI (-3.858, -0.083), p-adjusted=0.037; HE-AI mean difference -2.120, 95% CI (-4.049, -0.191), p-adjusted=0.025.
limitations: not reported in retrieved text (authors instead propose implications for practice/policy, e.g. designing multi-task and cross-context studies in the future, but do not state study limitations in retrieved text)
caveat_flags: essay score improvement is short-term performance proxy, not knowledge gain/transfer; lab-based task, real-classroom generalizability not addressed

title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
authors: Hamsa Bastani; Osbert Bastani; Alp Sungu; Haosen Ge; Özge Kabakcı; Rei Mariman
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
design: Preregistered randomized controlled trial (RCT), 3 arms (control, GPT Base, GPT Tutor), classroom-level randomization
n: "nearly 1,000 students" across "about fifty 9th, 10th, and 11th-grade classes"; main student-level regression uses 2,848 observations (student-level observations, not distinct students); problem-level specifications use 13,484 and 11,392 observations; 57 practice problems analysed for GPT error rates; per-arm Ns not reported in retrieved text
population: High school students (9th, 10th, and 11th grade) at a large high school in Turkey, Fall semester 2023–2024 academic year; minors (under 18)
ai_exposure: GPT-4 based tutoring tools: (1) "GPT Base" - a simple ChatGPT-like chat interface with a prompt indicating GPT-4 should serve as tutor and help solve the problem; (2) "GPT Tutor" - same interface but with guardrails: instructed to give hints without direct answers, and provided with teacher-supplied correct solutions and common student mistakes; (3) Control arm - no generative AI access, only course books/notes, no devices
measures: Normalized student performance (grade) on assisted practice problems (Practice perf) and unassisted closed-book exam (Exam perf), graded by independent graders using teacher-designed rubric; also self-reported student perceptions of performance/learning via end-of-session survey; Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI) as measure of grade dispersion; NLP clustering of student-AI chat messages to categorize engagement (superficial vs. nonsuperficial)
key_finding: Students in the GPT Tutor (resp., GPT Base) arm perform 127% (resp., 48%) better on the practice problems compared to students in the control arm. On the exam, students in the GPT Base arm perform statistically significantly worse than students in the control arm by 17%; this negative effect is essentially eradicated in the GPT Tutor arm, though the authors still do not observe a positive effect. Analysis of interactions suggests students use GPT Base as a "crutch" (asking for and copying solutions) while using GPT Tutor more substantively (asking for help or independently attempting answers). Students do not perceive any reduction in learning/performance from copying solutions, suggesting lack of awareness of how generative AI can impede their learning.
effect_size: Practice perf: GPT Base coefficient 0.137 (SE 0.031); GPT Tutor coefficient 0.361 (SE 0.032); control arm mean 0.284, control arm SD 0.287. Exam perf: GPT Base coefficient -0.054 (SE 0.022); GPT Tutor coefficient -0.004 (SE 0.013); control arm mean 0.321, control arm SD 0.277. Observations = 2,848; R2 practice = 0.389 (adjusted 0.382), R2 exam = 0.386 (adjusted 0.379). GPT Base correct answer rate: 51% average; logical errors 42% of time; arithmetic errors 8% of time. First-session first-interaction superficial rate: 56% GPT Base vs. 42% GPT Tutor; across all first interactions in first session: 67% GPT Base vs. 37% GPT Tutor.
limitations: The study focuses on two generative AI tutors for a single topic (mathematics) deployed in a single high school in Turkey; objective evaluation criteria for math problems are unavailable in other subjects such as writing; the deployment was carried out in Fall 2023 when generative AI was still very new, and modes of interaction may have changed as users become more familiar with these tools, and models have improved since then; the study focuses on short-term outcomes due to limitations imposed by the partner school, and studying long-term outcomes is a key direction for future research; while several analyses were performed to uncover mechanisms, the approach could be complemented with controlled experiments in settings with more fine-grained interventions and monitoring; five class sessions did not use the assigned treatment due to external circumstances (noncompliance).
caveat_flags: non-adult sample; single site; self-report component for perception measures; short-term outcomes only; no delayed retention test; generalizability limited to math/single school; noncompliance in five sessions

title: AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting
authors: Greg Kestin; Kelly Miller; Anna Klales; Timothy Milbourne; Gregorio Ponti
design: RCT, crossover design, randomised at peer-instruction group level (2–3 students), single course, IRB-approved
n: Total N=194 eligible (of 233 enrolled); post-test analysis: AI group N=142, in-class group N=174; combined pre-test N=316 (crossover design so students contribute to both conditions)
population: Undergraduate students in Physical Sciences 2 (PS2), an introductory physics course for life sciences at Harvard University, USA; adults (undergraduate university students)
ai_exposure: AI tutor ("PS2 Pal"), built via prompt engineering on GPT-4 with expert-crafted step-by-step solutions and structured guidance, used asynchronously at home, compared with in-class active learning (peer instruction/small-group activities with instructor feedback) on identical content; crossover so each student experienced both conditions in consecutive weeks on different topics (surface tension, fluid flow)
measures: Content mastery via pre-test and post-test quizzes on lesson-specific physics content (surface tension, fluid flow); prior physics background via midterm exam and Force Concept Inventory (FCI); scientific attitudes via CLASS survey; time on task (AI platform tracked); student perceptions of learning experience via four Likert-scale (1-5) statements on engagement, motivation, enjoyment, and growth mindset
key_finding: Students in the AI tutor group had significantly higher post-test scores and greater median learning gains (over double) relative to pre-test baseline compared with students in the in-class active learning group; a linear regression controlling for background measures, prior ChatGPT experience, crossover design factors, and time on task showed students in the AI group "performed substantially better on the post-test compared with those in the in-class active learning group," a highly significant result with a large effect size (noted as an underestimate due to ceiling effects, with quantile regression giving a larger estimate). There was no correlation between time on task and post-test scores. Students in the AI group also reported significantly greater engagement and motivation than the in-class group, while enjoyment and growth mindset ratings were comparable between groups.
effect_size: Post-test score comparison: median M=4.5 (AI, N=142) vs M=3.5 (in-class, N=174); pre-test combined M=2.75 (N=316); Mann-Whitney z = -5.6, p<10 [exponent not specified in text, likely truncated]; linear regression effect size = 0.63; quantile regression effect size range 0.73 to 1.3 standard deviations; engagement: AI Mean=4.1, SD=0.98 vs in-class Mean=3.6, SD=0.92, t(311) = -4.5, p<0.0001; motivation: AI Mean=3.4, SD=1.0 vs in-class Mean=3.1, SD=0.86, t(311) = -3.4, p<0.001; subgroup analyses by FCI score (below/above 40%) and CLASS score (below/above 65% benchmark): p<0.001; group-level clustered regression: p<0.001
limitations: Authors state: the AI tutoring approach was applied in a setting where students engaged substantially with material for the first time, with lessons at understanding/applying/analyzing levels of Bloom's Taxonomy; results may depend on factors such as a heterogeneous student population, integration of high-quality instructional videos, a capable LLM (GPT-4), expert-crafted question-specific prompts, and content suited to this format; they "do not presume that structured AI tutoring will always outperform in-class active learning in all contexts, for example, those requiring complex synthesis of multiple concepts and higher-order critical thinking"; accuracy relied on pre-written answers/solutions rather than the AI generating solutions independently; feedback was reactive to student input only, not multimodal or proactive; randomization was at the peer-instruction group level (2-3 students) rather than individual level, complicating interpretation of individual-level factors like time on task in the group-clustered model; significant overhead/time commitment was required to develop the AI tutor platform and prompts.
caveat_flags: single site; crossover design (order/carryover effects possible); randomisation at group level not individual level; ceiling effect noted by authors affecting effect size estimate; self-report measures for engagement/motivation/enjoyment/growth mindset; short-term outcome, no delayed retention test reported; narrow content domain (two physics topics); outcome is proxy not long-term learning

title: Experimental evidence of the effects of large language models versus web search on depth of learning
authors: Shiri Melumad; Jin Ho Yun
design: Series of 7 RCTs (4 in main text: Experiments 1-4, plus 3 preregistered replications); between-subjects, random assignment to search platform/condition; Experiments 1, 2, 4 preregistered (per text); Experiment 3 not stated as preregistered
n: Total across 7 experiments N=10,426 (as stated in intro). Exp 1: 1,136 recruited, 1,104 analyzed after exclusions (Google vs ChatGPT arms). Exp 2: 2,016 recruited, 1,979 analyzed (Google vs ChatGPT arms). Exp 3: 253 recruited, 250 analyzed (Google-standard vs Google-LLM/AI Overview arms). Exp 4: 1,501 recruited, 1,493 analyzed (recipients rating advice from 125 Google-link texts vs 125 AI Overview texts from Exp 3). Additional replications: n=2,402 (healthy lifestyle topic, 3 arms incl. LLM+web links), n=1,976 (financial scam topic), n=1,258 (conceptual replication of Exp 4)
population: Exp 1 & 2: Prolific panel members (online, adults - Exp1 mean age 42.40, SD 13.46; Exp2 mean age 41.28, SD 17.64); Exp 3: members of a behavioral lab panel at an east-coast US university, laboratory setting, adults (mean age 22.75, SD 8.65); Exp 4: MTurk Connect panel members, adults (mean age 39.79, SD 12.85). Country not explicitly stated beyond "east-coast university" (implying US); overall sample described as adults based on reported mean ages all well above 18
ai_exposure: LLM syntheses (ChatGPT/GPT-4o in Exp 1-2; Google's "AI Overview" LLM synthesis in Exp 3-4) versus traditional web search (Google search links). Exp1: actual interactive ChatGPT vs actual interactive Google search. Exp2: simulated ChatGPT summary vs simulated Google links, with identical underlying facts held constant across conditions. Exp3: Google's AI Overview summary vs standard Google web search links (search engine held constant). Exp4: recipients rated advice text previously generated by Exp3 participants who had used AI Overview vs web links (recipients themselves did not use AI tools, they evaluated outputs). Additional replications tested LLM (with and without real-time web links appended) vs web search.
measures: Self-reported depth of learning (Likert items: "I learned new things...", "comprehensive information...", "personal ownership over knowledge"); investment in advice formation (self-report items on thought/effort and ownership, plus time spent writing advice as behavioral proxy); time spent on search task (proxy for learning effort); number of queries submitted; advice content analyzed via NLP: word count (LIWC 2022), Named Entity Recognition for factual references (spaCy), topical similarity via LDA topic modeling + PCA + cosine similarity, semantic uniqueness via Levenshtein edit distance; structural equation model (SAS Proc Calis) testing mediation pathway; Experiment 4: recipient ratings of advice helpfulness, informativeness, perceived effort, trust, likelihood to recommend/adopt, plus forced-choice comparison and personal relevance index (Cronbach's alpha=0.806)
key_finding: Across seven experiments, participants who learned about a topic using LLM syntheses (vs. web links) exerted less effort in learning, reported developing shallower knowledge, were less invested in forming subsequent advice, and produced advice that was objectively sparser (fewer words, fewer factual references), less original/unique, and less trustworthy/informative to independent recipients, who were in turn less willing to adopt or recommend it. Effects held even when the search engine was held constant (Exp 3), when the underlying facts in the results were held constant and only presentation format varied (Exp 2), and when LLM summaries were augmented with real-time web links. The authors frame these as experimentally caused effects of the search-result format ("random assignment," "results support the predicted effects") but explicitly hedge learning depth as based on "participants' self-reported lower depth of learning" and note the effects are specific to the tested task context (learning to form advice), not necessarily generalizing to all learning contexts (e.g., specialized domains or factual lookup tasks).
limitations: Authors note: findings arose in a specific experimental task context (learning to form advice to share with others) and different LLM applications may yield different results (e.g., no obvious advantage of web search over LLM for simple factual lookup); task contexts did not require deep prior knowledge, so effects "might not generalize... to learning in highly specialized domains—such as advanced science or math topics—where LLM syntheses might better help users comprehend and interpret complex topics compared with web links"; evidence centered on participants' self-reported lower depth of learning, shorter/less factual advice text, and recipients' perceptions, but "there may well be other metrics of learning—such as performance on standardized tests—where LLMs offer advantages over web search"; in Experiment 2, repeated exposure to information across multiple websites (rather than solely search effort) may have contributed to the Google-condition advantage, though authors report the effect was sustained after controlling for number of websites visited (reported in supplement); potential confound in Experiments 1-2 that Google and ChatGPT differ in familiarity/novelty to users beyond just result format, addressed via Experiment 3's AI Overview design.
caveat_flags: preregistered (Exps 1, 2, 4 stated; Exp 3 and some replications not stated as preregistered); self-report measures used alongside behavioral/text proxies; outcome is proxy not learning (time spent, word count, NLP metrics as proxies for depth of learning); no delayed retention test; single university lab site for Experiment 3; MTurk/Prolific online panel samples; advice-writing task may not generalize to other learning contexts (authors' own caveat); supplementary material contains additional experiments not fully detailed in supplied text; text truncated (some numeric details e.g. exact chi-square degrees of freedom formatting garbled in source)

title: Generative AI and Learning Dynamics in Higher Education: A Longitudinal Empirical Study
authors: Chrysanthi Melanou; Maik Beege; Martin Kimmig
design: quasi-experimental longitudinal design, three parallel classes assigned to instructional conditions, measured at three time points (T1–T3)
n: 87 students at baseline (Group A=33, B=28, C=26); valid cases varied by measurement point and construct (e.g., T1 knowledge n=81, T3 knowledge n=62; RQ1 knowledge-gain analysis …
population: business informatics students in higher education; country/setting not reported in retrieved text; age not reported in retrieved text (likely adults given university context, but not stated)
ai_exposure: Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT; three conditions: tutor-AI use, unguided AI use, and a control group without AI
measures: Knowledge (T1, T3): behavioral/performance-based (14-item multiple true-false test scored for correct decisions). Motivation, Cognitive Load (ICL/ECL/GCL), Critical Thinking, Reflective Use (T1/T2/T3 as applicable): self-report Likert-scale questionnaires. Final school grade and AI experience (T1): self-reported/archival indicators. No physiological measures were used.
key_finding: Students showed significant knowledge gains across all groups, but no additional benefits of AI integration. Motivation remained largely stable; germane cognitive load increased and was positively associated with knowledge gain. Critical thinking remained stable, while reflective use was higher in the AI condition and positively associated with critical thinking. No evidence emerged for a Matthew effect, indicating that AI did not intensify performance inequalities. Overall, the findings did not support the view of generative AI as a consistent learning outcome; its impact depended on pedagogical framing and learners' metacognitive regulation.
effect_size: Abstract/Table 1 report: "Students showed significant knowledge gains across all groups, but no additional benefits of AI integration." Per Table 1: H1a (knowledge significantly increases T1→T3) = Supported/Yes; H1b (knowledge gains do not vary significantly across instructional conditions AI vs. control) = Supported/Yes; H1c (prior achievement/AI experience moderate gains consistent with a Matthew effect) = Not supported/No. The exact effect sizes, CIs, and p-values for these tests are reported in the Results section (3.1 RQ1) of the paper, which falls within the portion of the full text marked '[MIDDLE OMITTED]' in the provided excerpt and so cannot be quoted verbatim here.
limitations: not reported in retrieved text
caveat_flags: quasi-experimental (non-randomised); single site (three classes, one institution); N<100; age not reported

title: Endoscopist deskilling risk after exposure to artificial intelligence in colonoscopy: a multicentre, observational study
authors: Krzysztof Budzyń; Marcin Romańczyk; Diana Kitala; Paweł Kołodziej; Marek Bugajski; Hans‐Olov Adami; Johannes Blom; Marek Buszkiewicz; Natalie Halvorsen; Cesare Hassan; Tomasz Romańczyk; Øyvind Holme; Krzysztof Jarus; Shona Fielding; Melina A. Kunar; María Pellisé; Nastazja Pilonis; Michał F. Kamiński; Mette Kalager; Michael Bretthauer; Yuichi Mori
design: retrospective, observational, multicentre; before/after comparison across two 3-month phases pre/post AI implementation
n: 1443 colonoscopies (unit is colonoscopies, not distinct participants explicitly confirmed); n=795 before AI exposure, n=648 after AI exposure
population: patients undergoing diagnostic colonoscopy at four endoscopy centres in Poland (ACCEPT trial sites); median age 61 years (IQR 45-70); 847 (58.7%) female, 596 (41.3%) male; adults implied by age range but 'adults' not explicitly stated in retrieved text
ai_exposure: endoscopists at centres that introduced AI tools for polyp detection at end of 2021; outcome examined is their performance on non-AI assisted colonoscopy before vs after this AI exposure period
measures: adenoma detection rate (ADR) of standard, non-AI assisted colonoscopy, compared before vs after AI implementation; multivariable logistic regression to identify independent factors affecting ADR
key_finding: The ADR of standard colonoscopy decreased significantly from 28.4% before to 22.4% after exposure to AI; authors interpret this as continuous exposure to AI might reduce the ADR of standard non-AI assisted colonoscopy, suggesting a negative effect on endoscopist behaviour
effect_size: ADR before: 28.4% (226 of 795); ADR after: 22.4% (145 of 648); absolute difference -6.0% (95% CI -10.5 to -1.6; p=0.0089); multivariable logistic regression: AI exposure odds ratio 0.69 (95% CI 0.53-0.89); male vs female sex 1.78 (1.38-2.30); age >=60 vs <60 years 3.60 (2.74-4.72)
limitations: not reported in retrieved text
caveat_flags: retrospective observational design, not randomised for this comparison; before/after comparison, not a concurrent control group for the deskilling effect itself; single country (Poland), four centres; outcome is proxy (ADR) not direct measure of endoscopist cognitive skill or learning; authors' stated limitations not included in retrieved abstract text; funding source not fully assessed for conflicts (European Commission and Japan Society for the Promotion of Science funded)

title: Artificial Intelligence-Induced Deskilling in Interventional Pulmonology: An International Cross-Sectional Survey on Risk Perception and Mitigation Strategies
authors: Gianluca Marchi; Lorenzo Corbetta
design: international observational cross-sectional questionnaire-based survey (not stated as preregistered)
n: 118 participants (response rate 78.7% of 150 invited); 12 respondents each from 8 countries, 11 each from 2 countries (Morocco and Spain)
population: interventional pulmonologists (practicing specialists) from 10 countries: Australia, Canada, France, India, Italy, Morocco, Spain, Turkey, the United Kingdom, and the United States; age not reported as adults explicitly but age groups given (<35, 35–44, 45–54, ≥55 years) indicating adults
ai_exposure: Not an experimental exposure/manipulation; survey asked respondents about perceptions of AI in interventional pulmonology (e.g., AI-assisted lung nodule detection, robotic/computer-aided bronchoscopic navigation, AI-enhanced EBUS interpretation, ML-supported cytopathology, decision-support for pleural procedures) and their concerns/attitudes toward AI-induced deskilling; no arms/conditions—single cross-sectional sample rating 12 Likert items

effect_size: Q1: 87% (n=103); Q2: 73% (n=86); Q3: 38% (n=45); Q4: 81% (n=96); Q5: 83% (n=98); Q6: 84% (n=99); Q7: 86% (n=101); Q8: 78% (n=92); Q9: 77% (n=91); Q10: 89% (n=105); Q11: 74% (n=87); Q12: 70% (n=83). Explanation, AI confidence, and participant type were not significant moderators.
effect_size: Human–AI synergy (baseline = best of human alone or AI alone): g = −0.23; t = −2.89; two-tailed p = 0.005; 95% CI, −0.39 to −0.07 (I2 = 97.7%). Human augmentation (baseline = human alone): g = 0.64; t = 11.87; two-tailed p = 0.000; 95% CI, 0.53 to 0.74 (I2 = 93.8%). Task type moderation of synergy: F = 7.84, two-tailed p = 0.006. Decision tasks synergy: g = −0.27; t = −3.20; p = 0.002; 95% CI, −0.44 to −0.10. Creation tasks synergy: g = 0.19; t = 1.35; p = 0.180; 95% CI, −0.09 to 0.48 (n=34 effect sizes). Data type moderation: synergy F = 15.24, p = 0.000; augmentation F = 6.52, p = 0.000. Relative human/AI performance moderation: synergy F = 81.79, p = 0.000; augmentation F = 24.35, p = 0.000. When human>AI: synergy g = 0.46; t = 5.06; p = 0.000; 95% CI, 0.28 to 0.66. When AI>human: synergy g = −0.54; t = −6.20; p = 0.000; 95% CI, −0.71 to −0.37. Augmentation when AI>human: g = 0.74; t = 13.50; p = 0.000; 95% CI, 0.63 to 0.85. AI type moderation of synergy: F = 3.77, p = 0.026. Year of publication moderation of synergy: F = 3.65, p = 0.015. Experimental design moderation of augmentation: F = 4.90, p = 0.029. Predetermined delegation subtasks (3 experiments, 4 effect sizes): synergy g = 0.22; t = 0.69; p = 0.494; 95% CI, −0.42 to 0.87. Sensitivity analyses (paper-level clustering): synergy g = −0.22; t = −2.46; p = 0.017; 95% CI, −0.41 to −0.04; augmentation g = 0.65; t = 9.96; p = 0.000; 95% CI, 0.52 to 0.78. Outlier-excluded: synergy g = −0.25; t = −3.45; p = 0.001; 95% CI, −0.39 to −0.11; augmentation g = 0.60; t = 12.60; p = 0.000; 95% CI, 0.50 to 0.69. Leave-one-out ranges: synergy g from −0.28 to −0.19 (p 0.000–0.019); augmentation g from 0.61 to 0.66 (p 0.000). Excluding estimated (digitized) effect sizes: synergy g = −0.21; t = −2.59; p = 0.011; 95% CI, −0.36 to −0.05; augmentation g = 0.64; t = 11.73; p = 0.000; 95% CI, 0.53 to 0.75. Egger's regression for synergy: z = −0.67; two-tailed p = 0.438; 95% CI, −2.39 to 1.04. Egger's regression for augmentation: z = 1.96; two-tailed p = 0.002; 95% CI, 0.76 to 3.16.
limitations: Authors state: (1) quantitative results apply only to the subset of studies meeting inclusion criteria requiring reported human-alone, AI-alone, and human-AI performance, excluding tasks neither could perform alone; (2) effect sizes correspond to different quantitative measures (accuracy, error, quality) and come from different samples (doctors, crowdworkers, students), limiting comparability; measurement error varies across experiments (e.g., some studies use as many as 500 images, others as few as 15) and this was not accounted for in the weighting; (3) although no evidence of publication bias was found for synergy, it remains possible bias exists, though authors argue a bias favoring positive results seems unlikely given their negative overall finding; potential evidence of publication bias was found for human augmentation results; (4) results only apply to tasks, processes, and participant pools researchers chose to study, which may not represent real-world configurations (possible research topic selection bias); (5) quality of analysis depends on quality of synthesized studies; rigour may vary (e.g., different attention check mechanisms and incentive structures); (6) high heterogeneity among effect sizes remains largely unexplained by investigated moderators; potential interaction effects (e.g., explanation and AI type) could not be detected due to insufficient studies; other unanalyzed moderators (e.g., differing experimental platforms and stimuli) may introduce variation.
caveat_flags: meta-analysis of heterogeneous studies; high heterogeneity (I2 97.7% and 93.8%); potential publication bias for human augmentation outcome; population/age not explicitly reported; outcome relies on varying measures across studies (accuracy/error/quality); small subsample for creation-task effect (n=34, non-significant); very small subsample for delegation subtasks analysis (3 experiments, 4 effect sizes, non-significant); some effect sizes estimated via digitization or author contact

title: Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning
authors: Ethan Goh; Robert Gallo; Jason Hom; Eric Strong; Yingjie Weng; Hannah Kerman; Joséphine A. Cool; Zahir Kanjee; Andrew S. Parsons; Neera Ahuja; Eric Horvitz; Daniel X. Yang; Arnold Milstein; Andrew Olson; Adam Rodman; Jonathan H. Chen
design: Randomized, single-blind, stratified, multi-site clinical trial (RCT) comparing LLM vs conventional resources; case-level clustered analysis; also secondary LLM-alone comparison arm
n: 50 participants total (25 LLM group, 25 control group); unit of analysis also includes cases: 244 cases completed (125 LLM group, 119 control group); LLM-alone arm: 3 runs per case
population: US-licensed physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents) recruited from Stanford University, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, and University of Virginia; adults (practicing physicians); median years in practice 3 (IQR, 2-8)
ai_exposure: Intervention group used commercial LLM chatbot (ChatGPT Plus [GPT-4]; OpenAI) as diagnostic aid alongside any conventional resources; control group used conventional diagnostic resources (eg, UpToDate, Google) and were explicitly instructed not to use LLMs; secondary comparison arm used the LLM alone (0-shot prompt, run 3 times) to answer cases without human input
measures: Primary outcome: score (%) on an adapted structured reflection tool/grid (differential diagnosis, supporting/opposing findings, final diagnosis, next steps) scored by blinded raters. Secondary outcomes: time spent per case (seconds); final diagnosis accuracy (ordinal: incorrect/partially correct/most correct, and binary: incorrect vs at least partially correct). Assessment tool validation via weighted Cohen κ and Cronbach α.
key_finding: Physician use of a commercially available LLM chatbot did not improve diagnostic reasoning performance (structured reflection score) compared with conventional resources; no significant differences were found in time spent per case or final diagnosis accuracy. However, the LLM alone significantly outperformed both physician groups on diagnostic performance score. Subgroup analyses by training level and LLM experience were qualitatively similar to the whole cohort.
effect_size: Primary outcome: median score 76% (IQR, 66%-87%) LLM group vs 74% (IQR, 63%-84%) control; mixed-effects model difference 2 percentage points (95% CI, −4 to 8 percentage points; P=.60). Sensitivity analysis (all cases): difference 2 percentage points (95% CI, −4 to 8 percentage points; P=.50). Time: median 519 (IQR, 371-668) s LLM vs 565 (IQR, 456-788) s control; adjusted difference −82 seconds (95% CI, −195 to 31 seconds; P=.20) [Table 3 reports P=.15 for all participants]. Ordinal diagnosis accuracy: odds ratio 1.4 (95% CI, 0.7-2.8; P=.39). Binary diagnosis accuracy: odds ratio 1.9 (95% CI, 0.9-4.0; P=.10). LLM alone: median score 92% (IQR, 82%-97%); absolute score difference vs control 16 percentage points (95% CI, 2-30 percentage points; P=.03) favoring LLM alone. Weighted Cohen κ = 0.66; overall Cronbach α = 0.64 (0.67 after removing final diagnosis component).
limitations: Focused on a single LLM (commercial availability), though noted as among the most performant tools studied; participants had no explicit training in prompt engineering, which "could have improved the quality of their interactions with the system" but this was said to be consistent with current real-world integrations; physicians in the LLM arm were not forced to use the system in any consistent way (purposeful design for effectiveness evaluation); only 6 clinical vignettes used, which cannot comprehensively cover the variety of cases in medicine; cases were curated/summarized by human clinicians and the study was "acontextual," not capturing competence in patient interviewing/data collection or the clinical environment.
caveat_flags: multi-site but small N; N<30 per subgroup in some analyses; no delayed retention test; outcome is proxy not learning (rubric score vs downstream clinical impact not assessed); self-selected/volunteer sample; acontextual task per authors; no prompt-engineering training provided
