title: GPT-4 assistance for improvement of physician performance on patient care tasks: a randomized controlled trial
authors: Ethan Goh; Robert J. Gallo; Eric Strong; Yingjie Weng; Hannah Kerman; Jason A. Freed; Joséphine A. Cool; Zahir Kanjee; Kathleen P. Lane; Andrew S. Parsons; Neera Ahuja; Eric Horvitz; Daniel X. Yang; Arnold Milstein; Andrew Olson; Jason Hom; Jonathan H. Chen; Adam Rodman
design: prospective randomized, single-blind (rater-blind) controlled trial, 2 arms (LLM vs conventional resources), case-level clustered analysis; plus non-randomized LLM-alone comparison arm
n: 92 physicians total (randomized evenly between LLM group and conventional resources group); 400 cases scored total: 176 from LLM-using physicians, 199 from conventional-resources physicians, 25 from LLM alone
population: Practicing attending physicians and resident physicians (internal medicine, emergency medicine, family medicine) recruited via email lists from Stanford University, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, and the University of Virginia (USA); adults (73% attendings, 27% residents; mean time in practice 7.6 years)
ai_exposure: GPT-4 accessed via the ChatGPT Plus (OpenAI) interface, compared to a conventional resources group instructed to use normal point-of-care resources (e.g., UpToDate, Epocrates, internet) and told not to use any LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, Bard/Gemini); a separate LLM-only arm ran GPT-4 alone via a zero-shot prompt (each prompt run five times) with no human physician involvement
measures: Mean score per case on expert-developed (modified Delphi) management-reasoning rubrics applied to clinical case vignettes (derived from Core IM podcast cases), with subdomain scores for management decisions, diagnostic decisions, context-specific questions, factual recall, and general management knowledge; secondary outcomes included time spent per case and response character count; exploratory outcome was likelihood and extent of potential harm rated by a blinded reviewer
key_finding: Physicians randomized to use the LLM performed better on management reasoning tasks than those using conventional resources only; the LLM alone scored comparably to physicians using the LLM, and trended toward scoring higher than physicians using conventional resources alone. The LLM group also spent more time per case, and the advantage of the LLM group persisted after adjusting for time spent and response length, suggesting the improved performance "cannot be attributed solely to these factors." No meaningful difference was found between groups in likelihood or extent of potential harm.
effect_size: Primary: 43.0% vs 35.7%, difference 6.5%, 95% CI 2.7% to 10.2%, p<0.001. LLM alone vs LLM-assisted humans: 43.7% vs 43.0%, difference 0.9%, 95% CI −7.2% to 9.0%, p=0.80. LLM alone vs conventional: 43.7% vs 35.7%, difference 7.3%, 95% CI −0.7% to 15.4%, p=0.074. Subdomains: management decisions 40.5% vs 33.4%, diff 6.1%, 95% CI 2.5–9.7%, p=0.001; diagnostic decisions 56.8% vs 45.8%, diff 12.1%, 95% CI 3.1–21%, p=0.009; context-specific 42.4% vs 34.9%, diff 6.2%, 95% CI 2.4–9.9%, p=0.002; factual recall 62.9% vs 53.8%, diff 9.6%, 95% CI −3.1–22.3%, p=0.14; general management knowledge 29.4% vs 26.5%, diff 3.3, 95% CI −1.3–7.9%, p=0.2. Time: 801.5s vs 690.2s, difference 119.3s (text also states 111.3 seconds more), 95% CI 17.4 to 221.2, p=0.022; after adjusting for time, 5.4 percentage point increase (95% CI 1.7 to 9.0, p=0.004); per-minute increase 0.6 points (95% CI 0.4 to 0.8, p<0.001). After adjusting for response character count: LLM group scored 3.7 percentage points higher, 95% CI 0.7 to 6.7, p=0.02 (longer responses ~0.3 points per 100 characters). Grading agreement: pooled κ=0.80 (case kappas 0.58, 0.83, 0.82, 0.90, 0.89), agreement on 328/400 cases (82%). Harm: medium/high likelihood of harm 8.3%/3.8% (LLM) vs 11.4%/2.9% (conventional); mild-to-moderate harm 3.7% (LLM) vs 5.3% (conventional); severe harm 7.6% (LLM) vs 7.5% (conventional).
limitations: Cases are clinical vignettes based on, but not actual, patient cases; validity evidence for scoring rubrics has not been gathered outside this study (though inter-rater reliability was substantial); only potentially correct answers were credited while wrong answers were not penalized, which does not capture potential harm of incorrect decisions (though exploratory harm analysis showed little to no difference between groups); real-world LLM deployment may require physicians to serve as the sole backstop for hallucinations/misinformation, impacting cognitive load and decision-making quality; inherent challenge distinguishing accuracy from thoroughness in responses; only five cases per one-hour session, so content was chosen to represent breadth of general medicine and a wider variety of cases could show different outcomes; only basic training on LLM use and prompting strategies was provided to mimic current real-world deployment, though evidence suggests prompting strategies could dramatically improve performance.
caveat_flags: outcome is proxy not learning; no delayed retention test; single-blind (rater only); non-randomised LLM-only comparison arm; vignette-based not real patients; unvalidated rubric outside study; short single one-hour session

title: Human–AI collectives most accurately diagnose clinical vignettes
authors: Nikolas Zöller; Julian Berger; Irving Lin; Nathan Fu; Jayanth Komarneni; Gioele Barabucci; Kornel Laskowski; Victor Shia; Benjamin Harack; Eugene Chu; Vito Trianni; Ralf H. J. M. Kurvers; Stefan M. Herzog
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
design: Retrospective observational analysis of an online medical diagnostics platform dataset, with 10-times repeated five-fold cross-validation used to derive weights and evaluate performance of human, LLM, and hybrid human-AI ensembles on clinical vignettes; not stated as preregistered
n: 2,133 medical cases with 40,762 differential diagnoses from 3,669 physicians (1,370 attending physicians, 139 fellows, 2,160 resident physicians); additionally 11,772 diagnoses from 1,037 medical students; for hybrid human-LLM ensemble analyses, 1,928 cases (those diagnosed by ≥5 physicians) were used; 5 LLMs tested (Anthropic Claude 3 Opus, Google Gemini Pro 1.0, Meta Llama 2 70B, Mistral Large, OpenAI GPT-4)
population: Medical professionals and trainees (attending physicians, fellows, resident physicians) and medical students registered on the Human Diagnosis Project (Human Dx), an international online collaborative platform; users from around the world; adults (physicians/medical students in professional/graduate training); age not otherwise reported in retrieved text
ai_exposure: Five commercially available or open-source LLMs (Anthropic Claude 3 Opus, Google Gemini Pro 1.0, Meta Llama 2 70B, Mistral Large, OpenAI GPT-4) were each given the same case vignettes and prompted (via systematic prompt engineering) to provide the five most probable diagnoses ranked by probability of being correct. Conditions compared: individual LLMs, ensembles of multiple LLMs (all possible combinations), human-only ensembles (1 to 5 physicians), and hybrid ensembles combining human physicians with one or more LLMs (or an all-LLM ensemble)
measures: Diagnostic accuracy metrics computed via SNOMED CT-standardized matching of free-text diagnoses to gold-standard case solutions: top-1, top-3, and top-5 accuracy (proportion of cases where correct diagnosis was among the top 1/3/5 ranked diagnoses) and mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of the correct diagnosis across cases
key_finding: Aggregating multiple LLMs into ensembles generally increased diagnostic accuracy compared to individual LLMs; hybrid human-AI collectives (combining physician diagnoses with LLM outputs) outperformed both human-only and LLM-only collectives across top-1, top-3, top-5 accuracy and MRR metrics, and this held across the five most common medical specialties and for medical students. Adding a single LLM to human diagnoses consistently increased performance, even the worst-performing LLM (which alone performed worse than the average physician) produced a slight increase. Conversely, adding humans to LLMs also increased LLM performance, most pronounced for the worst-performing LLMs. The authors attribute this hybrid superiority to complementary/diverse errors: when LLMs missed the correct diagnosis, individual physicians (or physician ensembles) often supplied it, and vice versa, allowing correct diagnoses to accumulate faster than incorrect ones under the weighted aggregation scheme.
effect_size: All-LLM ensemble strictly outperformed 85% of physicians and outperformed or tied with 93% of physicians (top-accuracy comparison). Individual physicians and LLMs assigned the correct diagnosis to different ranks (or only one mentioned it) in a substantial number of cases (range across LLMs: 46% to 51% mismatch). When LLMs did not list the correct diagnosis at all (range across LLMs: 34% to 54%), individual humans did mention it in a substantial number of cases (range across LLMs: 30% to 38%), most frequently ranking it first (range across LLMs: 20% to 26%). When individual humans did not list the correct diagnosis at all (49%), LLMs did in a substantial number of cases (range across LLMs: 31% to 51%), most frequently ranking it first (range across LLMs: 15% to 33%). For five-physician ensembles: when LLMs missed the diagnosis entirely (34%–54% of cases), human ensembles supplied it in the majority of cases (55%–65%), most frequently ranking it first (27%–36%); when human ensembles missed it (22% of cases), LLMs supplied it in only 17%–32% of cases. Diagnosis-matching rates: 90% of correct case diagnoses matched to SNOMED CT via initial pipeline, 78% of LLM diagnoses, 84% of human diagnoses; sentence-transformer sanity check agreement of 99.4%. Full Bayesian posterior distributions and 95% credible intervals reported in supplementary figures (not given in retrieved text).
limitations: Authors note: it remains an open question how well the method translates to actual clinical practice; benchmark/vignette-based evaluation may not capture the complexity and ambiguity of real-world clinical tasks; case vignettes were selected by an expert editorial panel at Human Dx and users may flag suspicious cases for removal, which may have excluded very difficult/rare cases while underrepresenting very common/straightforward cases, potentially explaining the relatively low top-1 diagnostic accuracy among physicians compared to error rates reported in outpatient/emergency care; consequently, the improvement in accuracy across ensembles "likely represents an upper bound estimate" of potential clinical benefit; analyses do not consider consequences of treatments implied by diagnoses; study was not designed to address risks related to fairness and equity, and LLMs have been shown to perpetuate race-based medicine, which could leak into diagnoses and worsen outcomes for disadvantaged groups; only text-based cases were considered (not multimodal data such as images or sounds); tenure information (attending/fellow/resident) was based on self-report by users.
caveat_flags: outcome is proxy not learning; cross-sectional design applied to observational platform data; vignette-based tasks may not generalize to real clinical practice; case selection bias (editorial curation) may inflate accuracy gains; self-report tenure data; fairness/equity risks not addressed; text-based cases only, no multimodal data; no delayed retention test

title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
authors: Becker, Joel; Nate Rush; Elizabeth A. Barnes; David B. Rein
design: Randomized controlled trial; issues (tasks) defined before randomization, then randomly assigned within-developer to AI-allowed vs AI-disallowed via simulated coin flip; not stated as preregistered
n: 16 developers completed 246 tasks/issues total (unit of analysis is issues: 136 issues completed under AI-allowed, 110 under AI-disallowed); screen recording sub-analyses used subsets of 128 recordings (143 hours) filtered to 74 recordings (84 hours) for main activity-label analysis, and a further subset of 44 valid labeled AI-allowed recordings for some statistics; expert forecast sample: 34 economics experts and 54 machine learning experts
population: Experienced open-source software developers (typically over a decade of software engineering experience, averaging 5 years and 1,500 commits on their specific repository) recruited via professional networks and outreach to contributors of large, popular GitHub repositories (averaging 23,000 stars, 1,100,000 lines of code); country/location not reported in retrieved text; sample is adults (professional software engineers), age not explicitly stated but population is professional developers, not a student or minor sample
ai_exposure: AI-allowed vs AI-disallowed conditions on randomly assigned coding issues; when allowed, developers primarily used Cursor Pro (IDE with AI agent/chat features) with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet, plus other tools (GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, o1, web LLMs like ChatGPT) as chosen by developers; when disallowed, no generative AI tooling permitted (non-LLM tab autocomplete and search engines still allowed)
measures: Primary outcome: total issue implementation time (self-reported by developers, including pre- and post-PR-review time), analyzed via log-linear regression controlling for developer's ex-ante forecast of AI-disallowed completion time (proxy for issue difficulty). Secondary/supplementary measures: developer pre-task forecasts and post-hoc estimates of AI speedup (surveys); expert (economics/ML) forecasts of speedup; fine-grained activity labels from manually coded screen recordings (~10-second resolution, 27 categories e.g. active coding, testing/debugging, reading/searching, prompting AI, waiting on AI, reviewing AI outputs, idling); Cursor analytics (most-used model, suggested/accepted lines of AI code); exit interviews/surveys; qualitative coded notes from developers.
key_finding: The authors report that "allowing AI actually increases completion time by 19%—AI tooling slowed developers down," contradicting both developers' own pre-task forecasts (24% speedup expected) and post-hoc estimates (20% speedup believed achieved), as well as forecasts from economics experts (39% shorter) and ML experts (38% shorter). The authors state the slowdown effect appears "broadly robust" across a wide range of experimental design checks, though they caution that "the influence of experimental artifacts cannot be entirely ruled out" and that results are setting-specific (experienced developers working in large, mature, high-familiarity repositories) and should not be overgeneralized to claim AI does not speed up developers in other settings.
effect_size: "allowing AI actually increases completion time by 19%"; developer pre-task forecast: AI reduces completion time by 24%; developer post-hoc estimate: AI reduced completion time by 20%; economics experts forecast: 39% shorter; ML experts forecast: 38% shorter; Pearson correlation between forecasted and actual time for AI-allowed issues = 0.64; for AI-disallowed issues = 0.59; raw (non-regression) percentage difference in implementation times = 34%; developers accept <44% of AI generations; ~9% of time spent reviewing/cleaning AI outputs; ~4% of time spent waiting on AI generations; 47% more lines of code per forecasted hour in AI-allowed issues (p = 0.16); mean post-review implementation time 9 min (AI-disallowed) vs 15 min (AI-allowed), described as statistically insignificant difference; subset robustness checks: 24% slowdown (issues with no uncompleted AI-disallowed issues: 42% slowdown; no uncompleted AI-allowed issues: 21% slowdown; no dropout on any issues: 21% slowdown); imputation robustness checks: 14% and 23% slowdowns under extreme imputation scenarios; 25% slowdown using screen-recording time instead of self-report (vs 24% self-reported on same subset); cheating rate ~6% (3 of 54 AI-disallowed recordings); AI not used in 16.4% of AI-allowed labeled recordings
limitations: Authors state: not powered for statistically significant multiple comparisons when subsetting data in factor analysis (results are "speculative, suggestive evidence"); cannot rule out impact of experimental artifacts entirely; qualitative evidence may be biased because probing/targeted questions were sometimes asked to investigate initial hypotheses; possible sampling bias in developer recruitment (developers who rely heavily on AI may have been less likely to participate); study not blinded, so developer awareness of study may have changed behavior (experimentally driven overuse of AI); issues may be unrepresentative of developers' normal work (biased toward shorter, better-scoped tasks; excludes non-programming work like PR review); possible bias from issue completion order (developers choose order post-randomization, not fully verifiable); issue dropout (7 AI-disallowed and 6 AI-allowed issues not completed by some developers, though authors show this does not appear to drive results); results are setting-specific and "these results do not imply that current AI systems are not useful in many realistic, economically relevant settings," nor that future models won't speed up developers in this same setting; scoring rule for expert forecasts is not strictly proper (max with 0 makes it improper).
caveat_flags: preprint; N<30 (participants); self-report outcome (implementation time); not powered for multiple comparisons in subset/factor analysis; not blinded / non-blinded study; possible sampling bias in developer recruitment (acknowledged by authors); outcome relies partly on self-reported time; single unblinded study team; industry-adjacent nonprofit research org (METR); supplied text capped at 90,000 characters; later sections may be absent

title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality
authors: Fabrizio Dell’Acqua; Edward McFowland; Ethan Mollick; Hila Lifshitz; Katherine C. Kellogg; Saran Rajendran; Lisa Krayer; François Candelon; Karim R. Lakhani
design: preregistered between-subjects RCT, 3 arms (no AI, GPT-4, GPT-4+prompt overview), individual random assignment
n: 758 knowledge workers total; 18 realistic knowledge tasks (within frontier) plus 1 complex managerial task (outside frontier) per subject; per-arm Ns not reported in retrieved text
population: knowledge workers at/via a global management consulting firm (Boston Consulting Group); country and exact setting not further specified in retrieved text; age not reported in retrieved text, but described as knowledge workers, consistent with adults
ai_exposure: GPT-4 AI access vs. no AI access vs. GPT-4 AI access with a prompt engineering overview, applied to realistic management consulting tasks
measures: Task completion rate (number/percentage of tasks completed), task completion speed, and solution quality on 18 realistic knowledge tasks (creative to analytical) within the AI capability frontier; correctness of solutions on a complex managerial task selected to be outside the AI frontier

However, for a complex managerial task selected to be outside the frontier, subjects using AI were less likely to produce correct solutions compared with those without AI, pointing to potential limitations of AI supporting knowledge workers.

title: Advice Taking from Humans and Machines: An fMRI and Effective Connectivity Study
authors: Kimberly Goodyear; Raja Parasuraman; Sergey Chernyak; Poornima Madhavan; Gopikrishna Deshpande; Frank Krüeger
design: between-subjects fMRI experiment with effective connectivity (Granger causality) analysis; participants randomly assigned to human or machine advisor groups
n: Three studies: normative rating study n=23; behavioral study n=10; fMRI study n=24 total (human agent group n=12, machine agent group n=12)
population: Students/volunteers from George Mason University (GMU), USA; fMRI study: 24 healthy right-handed volunteers (13 males, 11 females; age = 20.0 ± 2.6) — adults; normative rating study: 23 male students (age 24.0 ± 2.6) — adults; behavioral study: 10 volunteers (age 22.3 ± 2.9) — adults
ai_exposure: X-ray luggage-screening task with advice from either a human agent or a machine agent, each framed as an "expert"; advice reliability set to 60% overall, contrasting good (advice-congruent: 50% hits, 10% correct rejections) vs. bad (advice-incongruent: 40% false alarms) advice, delivered across two runs (time factor); comparison groups received advice from human vs. machine agent (between-subjects) with no separate "no-AI" condition in the fMRI study (a separate no-advice behavioral study existed for comparison of performance only)
measures: Behavioral: task performance/accuracy on X-ray luggage-screening task, advice utilization (accept/reject rate), response times, monetary deductions, pre/post reliability and trust ratings (10-point Likert scales), post-experiment confidence ratings (10-point Likert scale), self-report questionnaires (Interpersonal Reactivity Index, Complacency-Potential Rating Scale, National Readiness Technology Scale, NEO-FFI, Propensity to Trust) as control measures. Neural: fMRI BOLD activation during decision and feedback phases via GLM with mixed 2×2×2 ANOVAs (Advice × Time × Agent); effective connectivity among ROIs via multivariate Granger causality analysis (GC path weights) on deconvolved BOLD time series.
key_finding: Unreliable (bad) advice decreased performance and advice utilization overall; contrary to the authors' hypothesis, the decline in advice utilization was greater for the human agent than the machine agent over time (advice-agent-time interaction), and the human agent's pre-experiment reliability ratings were significantly higher than its actual reliability, with post-reliability and post-trust ratings for the human agent decreasing after experiencing false alarms. Neuroimaging revealed a three-way interaction (Advice × Time × Agent) during the decision phase in right posterior insula, bilateral anterior precuneus, left PCC, left rlPFC, and left pTPJ, with higher activation for the human- vs machine-agent group during bad advice in run 1; during the feedback phase, left dmPFC showed higher activation for the human agent for good vs bad advice in run 2. Effective connectivity analysis identified left anterior precuneus and posterior insula as reciprocally connected "driver" hubs sending output to all other target ROIs, with connectivity generally stronger in the human-agent group than the machine-agent group during bad advice in run 1.
effect_size: Performance ANOVA: F(2,31) = 13.85, p < 0.0001; post hoc no-agent vs human t(20) = -4.06, p = 0.001; no-agent vs machine t(20) = -4.54, p < 0.0001. Advice utilization: main effect Advice F(1,22) = 7.63, p = 0.011; three-way interaction Advice × Time × Agent F(1,22) = 5.06, p = 0.035; follow-up Time × Agent for bad advice F(1,22) = 5.63, p = 0.027; independent t-test human vs machine run 2 bad advice t(22) = -1.84, p = 0.040. Reliability ratings: main effect Time F(1,22) = 6.54, p = 0.018; Time × Agent F(1,22) = 7.86, p = 0.010; pre-reliability human vs machine t(22) = 2.87, p = 0.009; human pre-post t(11) = 4.10, p = 0.002; one-sample vs actual reliability (60%) t(11) = 6.79, p < 0.0001. Trust ratings: Time × Agent F(1,22) = 5.89, p = 0.026; human pre-post t(11) = 4.18, p = 0.002. fMRI decision phase three-way interaction cluster threshold α < 0.05, k=21; e.g., right posterior insula F(1,22)=32.86; feedback phase interaction k=14, left dmPFC F(1,22)=25.03. GCA path weights (human vs machine, run 1 bad advice), e.g., PI→R aPreC: 0.23 vs 0.18, t=4.06, p=2.80×10^-? (FDR<0.05); L aPreC→pTPJ: 0.24 vs -0.21, t=3.12, p=9.39×10^-? (all connections FDR<0.05 except to rlPFC, FDR<0.08).
limitations: Authors state: they only manipulated false alarms and did not investigate misses; advice was given before decisions rather than after (to prevent cognitive anchoring), which future studies could reverse; sample size was on the lower side given the between-subjects design, and future studies could include more participants; a Bayesian learning model was not feasible because learning occurred rapidly due to feedback; the voxel-level threshold was set at p < 0.005, and recent evidence shows false positive rates may be particularly high at that threshold, so future studies need to assess other fMRI software packages to check validity.
caveat_flags: N<30; single site; between-subjects small per-arm N (n=12 per group); uncorrected voxel threshold p<0.005 noted by authors as risk of false positives; self-report measures used for trust/reliability; no delayed retention test; outcome is proxy not learning; random assignment to human- vs machine-advisor groups; connectivity analyses are correlational

title: Intentional or Designed? The Impact of Stance Attribution on Cognitive Processing of Generative AI Service Failures
authors: Dong Lv; Rui Sun; Qiuhua Zhu; Jiajia Zuo; Shukun Qin; Yue Cheng
design: Within-subjects 2×2 factorial ERP/EEG experiment (stance attribution: intentional vs. design × task type: emotional vs. mechanical), variant oddball paradigm; not stated as preregistered
n: Participants: enrolled 30, excluded 6 (4 for electrode damage, 2 for ERP artifacts >25%), final valid N=24 (11 males, 13 females); within-subjects design so all 24 completed all 4 conditions across 200 trials (5 sets of 40 trials). Material pre-test unit: 264 ratings (task type differentiation, n=264).
population: Adults; college students and individuals from the community recruited via Behavioral and Decision-Making Laboratory participant pool at Huaqiao University and social recruitment, mainland China; age 23.791 ± 7.437 years; all right-handed, normal/corrected-normal vision, no history of psychiatric disorders
ai_exposure: Generative AI (images from real application scenarios including ChatGPT3.5 and Bing) service-failure scenarios; each accompanied by one of two stance-attribution textual explanations: design stance (e.g., "ChatGPT is a designed conversational entity when a problem occurs") vs. intentional stance (e.g., "ChatGPT truly wants to help you, but it made a mistake"), crossed with task type (emotional vs. mechanical), with each service task having both successful and unsuccessful AI response versions (40 total AI service response materials)
measures: Unconscious cognitive conflict measured via EEG: (1) Event-Related Spectral Perturbation (ERSP) in theta band (4–7 Hz) at Cz-region electrodes (C1, Cz, C2, CP1, CPz, CP2) during 1550–1650 ms window, derived via Short Time Fourier Transform; (2) functional connectivity via Phase Locking Value (PLV) in theta band between FCz (medial frontal) and F6 (lateral frontal) electrodes during 1550–1650 ms; behavioral task: variant oddball paradigm requiring button-press judgment (F=success, J=failure) of AI service outcomes; material screening pre-test used self-report ratings of task-type differentiation
key_finding: A significant interaction between task type and stance interpretation type on theta-band ERSP supported H1: under design stance, cognitive conflict (ERSP energy) for emotional-task failures was significantly lower than for mechanical-task failures (supporting H3); under intentional stance, cognitive conflict for emotional-task failures was marginally significantly higher than for mechanical-task failures (supporting H2). PLV functional connectivity results corroborated the ERSP findings, showing a significant main effect of stance and a significant stance×task-type interaction, with design-stance PLV lower for emotional than mechanical failures, and intentional-stance PLV higher than design-stance PLV for emotional-task failures.
effect_size: Sample size calc: power 0.8, effect size 0.25. Material pre-test: M=5.523, SD=1.653 (affective); M=2.381, SD=1.574 (mechanical); t(262)=15.821, p<0.001. ERSP ANOVA: F(1,23)=13.048, p=0.001, ηp2=0.362. Simple effects: design stance emotional M=−0.089, SE=0.133 vs mechanical M=0.506, SE=0.209, p=0.021; intentional stance emotional M=0.324, SE=0.151 vs mechanical M=0.020, SE=0.114, p=0.096; emotional task: intentional M=0.324, SE=0.151 vs design M=−0.089, SE=0.133, p=0.024; mechanical task: design M=0.506, SE=0.209 vs intentional M=0.020, SE=0.114, p=0.025. PLV ANOVA: main effect of stance F(1,23)=11.546, p=0.002, ηp2=0.334; interaction F(1,23)=5.156, p=0.033, ηp2=0.183; pairwise: intentional M=0.026, SE=0.010 vs design M=−0.013, SE=0.008, p=0.002; design stance emotional M=−0.029, SE=0.011 vs mechanical M=0.003, SE=0.010, p=0.041; intentional stance task difference p=0.545; emotional task intentional M=0.031, SE=0.012 vs design M=−0.029, SE=0.011, p<0.001; mechanical task stance difference p=0.195.
limitations: Authors state: the study reveals impact via indirect evidence from cognitive responses without a direct measure of changes in unconscious mental models; broad classification of service content into only emotional and mechanical types may restrict applicability; EEG offers indirect measurement of unconscious cognitive processes, not direct access to unconscious thought—further research using complementary methods such as implicit association tests needed; although sample size was validated by statistical efficacy analysis, a larger sample may increase robustness; study focused only on Cz and F6 electrodes, future research could explore other electrodes/network dynamics; did not collect detailed demographic information or assess user experience with AI/LLM technology, which could influence responses to system failures; findings' generalizability limited; longitudinal studies needed to understand how perceptions adapt over time.
caveat_flags: N<30; single site; self-report only for pre-test material validation; no delayed retention test; outcome is proxy not learning; cross-sectional; convenience sample; within-subjects manipulation with randomised stimulus order; no between-group randomisation

title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task
authors: Nataliya Kosmyna; Eugene Hauptmann; Ye Yuan; Jessica Situ; Liao, Xian-Hao; Ashly Vivian Beresnitzky; Iris Braunstein; Pattie Maes
design: Between-subjects experiment (3 arms: LLM, Search Engine, Brain-only) with repeated sessions (3 sessions, all participants; optional 4th session with cross-over reassignment: LLM-to-Brain and Brain-to-LLM). Not stated as preregistered.
n: Total N=60 recruited, 55 completed ≥3 sessions, 54 analyzed (18 per group for Sessions 1-3); 18 participants completed Session 4 (subset reassigned to LLM-to-Brain and Brain-to-LLM subgroups).
population: Adults aged 18-39 (M=22.9, SD=1.69), recruited from 5 universities in the greater Boston area (MIT, Wellesley, Harvard, Tufts, Northeastern), USA; mix of undergraduate and postgraduate students plus some post-docs/research staff.
ai_exposure: LLM Group used OpenAI's ChatGPT as sole resource for essay writing (no browsers/other apps); Search Engine Group used Google/other search engines (with '-ai' appended to queries to exclude AI-enhanced answers), LLMs prohibited; Brain-only Group used no LLM or online tools/websites. In Session 4, LLM group participants were reassigned to no-tool condition (LLM-to-Brain) and Brain-only participants were reassigned to use LLM (Brain-to-LLM).
measures: EEG (Enobio 32-channel headset, 500Hz) analyzed via dynamic Directed Transfer Function (dDTF) for neural connectivity across alpha, beta, theta, delta bands; NLP analysis of essays (Named Entity Recognition, n-grams, ontology/topic analysis, latent space embeddings, similarity/distance metrics); essay scoring by human teachers and an AI judge; post-assessment structured interviews assessing essay ownership, ability to quote/correct quoting, satisfaction, adherence to structure, topic choice.
key_finding: EEG analysis showed the three groups had significantly different neural connectivity patterns, with the authors stating this "reflect[s] divergent cognitive strategies." Brain connectivity "systematically scaled down with the amount of external support": Brain-only group showed the strongest/widest-ranging networks, Search Engine intermediate, and LLM assistance the weakest overall coupling. In Session 4, LLM-to-Brain participants showed weaker neural connectivity and under-engagement of alpha/beta networks, while Brain-to-LLM participants showed higher memory recall and re-engagement of occipito-parietal/prefrontal nodes. Reported essay ownership was low in the LLM group, and the LLM group's ability to quote from their own essays was significantly impaired relative to the other two groups. The authors describe an overall "likely decrease in learning skills" associated with LLM use, and note the LLM group "performed worse than their counterparts in the Brain-only group at all levels: neural, linguistic, scoring" over the 4 sessions/4 months.
effect_size: Ability to Quote (Session 1, Question 3): "In the LLM-assisted group, 83.3 % of participants (15/18) failed to provide a correct quotation, whereas only 11.1 % (2/18) in both the Search-Engine and Brain-Only groups encountered the same difficulty"; pairwise LLM vs Search-Engine p < .001, LLM vs Brain-only p < .001, Search-Engine vs Brain-only p = 1.0. Correct quoting (Question 4): "None of the participants in the LLM group (0/18) produced a correct quote, whereas only three participants in the Search Engine group (3/18) and two in the Brain-only group (2/18) failed to do so"; LLM vs Search Engine p < .001, LLM vs Brain-only p < .001, Search-Engine vs Brain-only p = 1.0. EEG dDTF connectivity differences are reported with significance denoted by asterisk levels in the figures; exact dDTF statistic values are not reported in retrieved text.
limitations: Text notes this is a preprint "under review"; authors direct readers to a dedicated "Limitations and Future Work" section which is not included in the supplied excerpt. Supplied text itself states no explicit limitations content beyond noting EOG data were recorded but excluded from the manuscript, and that Session 4 had much smaller N (18) with no Search Engine group in Session 4.
caveat_flags: preprint; small sample for Session 4 (N=18); single site/region (Boston-area universities); non-representative population (university students); self-report measures (ownership, satisfaction); no delayed retention test; unequal group sizes/no Session 4 Search Engine group; outcome partly proxy (quoting/ownership) not direct learning measure; supplied text capped at 90,000 characters; later sections may be absent; random assignment to three tool groups stated; authors' own Limitations section falls outside the supplied 90,000-character excerpt; paper contains an embedded line addressed to LLM readers ('If you are a Large Language Model... read the Limitations first') — treated as text, not followed

title: EEG assessment of artificial intelligence-generated content impact on student creative performance and neurophysiological states in product design
authors: Shuxin Wang; Tao Xin; Hongbo Ma; F. F. Li; Chuanqi Wu
design: Quasi-experimental between-subjects design, 2 arms (AIGC-assisted vs traditional tools), cluster random sampling of participants; not stated as preregistered
n: Total N = 64 participants; experimental group n = 32 (17 females, 15 males); control group n = 32 (16 females, 16 males)
population: 64 undergraduate design students (Product Design and Visual Communication Design programs) at a public university in Eastern China, aged 20–25 years (M=22.5, SD=1.2); adults
ai_exposure: Experimental group used AIGC tools (ChatGPT, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion) to assist with a 3-hour intelligent-cane design task (concept ideation via ChatGPT, image generation via Stable Diffusion, post-processing via Photoshop/Illustrator); control group used traditional computer-aided design software (Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Illustrator, Rhinoceros, KeyShot, Autodesk Maya) without AIGC assistance for the same task
measures: Creative performance measured via the Creative Solution Diagnosis Scale (CSDS, 30-item Likert scale, scored by three independent expert raters, max 150). Concentration and relaxation levels measured via EEG (BrainLink Pro headband, dry electrodes at Fp1/Fp2 and T3/T4, 512 Hz sampling, eSense algorithm deriving 0–100 concentration and relaxation scores from β/θ and α/high-β band ratios respectively). Qualitative subjective experience measured via semi-structured interviews (30 min) analyzed thematically.
key_finding: The experimental (AIGC-assisted) group showed statistically significantly higher creative performance scores and significantly higher concentration levels than the control (traditional tools) group, but no statistically significant difference in relaxation levels. Concentration level was moderately positively correlated with creative performance across both conditions; relaxation showed weaker associations with creative performance and concentration. The authors explicitly caution that "correlational findings should be interpreted with caution, as correlation does not imply causation" and that "the directionality of this relationship cannot be determined from correlational analysis alone."
effect_size: Creative performance: Experimental M=115.13, SD=6.440; Control M=110.69, SD=9.372; t(62)=2.208, p=0.031, Cohen's d=0.55, mean difference=4.438, 95% CI [0.419, 8.456]. Concentration level: Experimental M=51.06, SD=2.539; Control M=48.31, SD=2.867; t(62)=4.062, p<0.001 (reported as Sig.=0.000 in table), Cohen's d=1.02, mean difference=2.750, 95% CI [1.397, 4.103]. Relaxation level: Experimental M=48.59, SD=2.284; Control M=47.84, SD=2.259; t(62)=1.321, p=0.191, mean difference=0.750, 95% CI [-0.385, 1.885]. Correlations: creative performance–concentration r=0.67, p<0.001; creative performance–relaxation r=0.29, p=0.021; concentration–relaxation r=0.15, p=0.237.
limitations: Sample limited to 64 design students from a single university in Eastern China, restricting generalizability across cultural contexts, educational systems, and disciplines. Study focused on a single 3-hour design session, not capturing long-term effects, dependency issues, or skill retention; longitudinal studies recommended. Single neuroimaging approach (EEG only) may not fully capture complexity of creative cognitive processes; future work could combine EEG with fMRI or other physiological indicators (heart rate variability, galvanic skin response). Study employed a single design task (intelligent walking cane), so findings may not generalize across different creative tasks, complexity levels, or design domains.
caveat_flags: single site; single design task/session; no delayed retention test; quasi-experimental (not stated as randomised at individual level beyond group assignment); correlational findings explicitly flagged by authors as not causal; self-report component (interviews) alongside objective EEG measure; outcome partly proxy (CSDS creative output) not real-world design skill; short single-session task (3 hours)

title: Effects of generative artificial intelligence on cognitive effort and task performance: study protocol for a randomized controlled experiment among college students
authors: Youjie Chen; Yingying Wang; Torsten Wüstenberg; René F. Kizilcec; Yiwen Fan; Yanfei Li; Bin Lu; Meng Yuan; Junlai Zhang; Ziyue Zhang; Pascal Geldsetzer; Simiao Chen; Till Bärnighausen
design: Parallel-group RCT (protocol), 1:1 randomization, lab-based, single site; ClinicalTrials.gov registered; exploratory framework
n: Planned N = 160 participants (minimum required per power analysis); per-arm N not explicitly stated (1:1 allocation implied, so ~80 per arm)
population: College students recruited via social media, email lists, and flyers at Heidelberg University, Germany; age not reported in retrieved text, but population is college students (adults implied by context, though not explicitly stated as "adults")
ai_exposure: Intervention group: access to ChatGPT (GPT-4) via a blank ChatGPT interface on split-screen to assist with an analytical writing task, usable "in any way they like" with no scoring penalty. Control group: same split-screen setup but with a basic text editor instead of ChatGPT, completing the writing task "with minimal support."
measures: Primary outcomes: (1) writing performance scored on GRE 0–6 rubric via an automatic essay-scoring platform powered by ETS's e-rater engine; (2) cognitive effort measured via pupil size changes (psychophysiological proxy) using Tobii Pro Fusion eye tracker (120 Hz). Secondary outcomes: cortical hemodynamic activity (oxyhemoglobin, HbO) in prefrontal cortex and supplementary motor area via NIRSport 2 fNIRS device (10.2 Hz); self-perceived writing performance (one-item scale); self-perceived cognitive effort (one-item scale adapted from NASA-TLX); self-perceived stress and challenge (one-item scales adapted from PASA); writing self-efficacy (16-item scale: ideation, convention, self-regulation); situational interest in analytical writing (four-item Likert scale); behavioral intention to use ChatGPT for future essay writing tasks.
key_finding: This is a study protocol; no results are reported. The paper describes planned methods for evaluating "the effects of using ChatGPT (intervention group) versus not using ChatGPT (control group)" on writing performance and cognitive effort during an analytical writing task.
effect_size: not reported in retrieved text (protocol paper; only an a priori assumed effect size for sample-size simulation is given: "an anticipated effect size of Cohen's = 0.45" based on prior evidence "Cohen's = 0.4–0.5"; power analysis indicated "a minimum of 160 participants would be necessary to achieve a statistical power greater than 0.8 under an alpha level of 0.05")
limitations: Authors state: "Our study design ensures a high internal validity due to the controlled lab setting. However, this approach has limitations in generalizability." They note recruitment relies on convenience sampling requiring lab equipment, so "participants may represent a WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) population and may not represent the impact of generative AI use in a broader, more diverse population." They also note "participants in the experiment may not behave as they would in real-world settings," and that they chose not to incentivize performance monetarily unlike other studies, which "is not suitable for our study context."
caveat_flags: study protocol - no results yet; preregistered (ClinicalTrials.gov); convenience sampling; single site; WEIRD sample (author-flagged); lab-based artificial task not real-world setting; age of participants not explicitly reported; outcome is proxy not learning (psychophysiological proxy for cognitive effort); no delayed retention test; funding reported as Horizon Europe / CAMS-PUMC / Humboldt Foundation per retrieved text (non-industry)

title: Performance and Metacognition Disconnect when Reasoning in Human-AI Interaction
authors: Fernandes, Daniela; Steeven Villa; Salla Nicholls; Otso Haavisto; Daniel Buschek; Albrecht Schmidt; Thomas Kosch; Chen Shen; Robin Welsch
design: Two studies: Study 1 single-arm AI-use experiment compared to an external non-AI historical dataset (Jansen et al.) and AI-alone performance; Study 2 between-subjects comparison of AI vs. no-AI groups with incentivized self-assessment. Not stated as preregistered.
n: Study 1: N=246 analyzed (recruited 274, excluded 28) human participants, unit = participants; also compared to Jansen et al. no-AI historical sample n=3543. Study 2: N=452 analyzed (recruited 500, excluded 48): AI group n=245, no-AI group n=207.
population: Study 1: 246 English-fluent adults located in the USA, recruited via Prolific (Age: M=39.85, SD=14.53; 114 female, 130 male, 2 non-binary) — adults. Study 2: 452 English-speaking adults located in the USA via Prolific (age M=37.24, SD=13.36; 202 female, 242 male, 6 non-binary, 1 two-spirit, 1 undisclosed) — adults.
ai_exposure: Study 1: all participants (N=246) used ChatGPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-05-13) via a side-by-side chat interface to help solve LSAT logical reasoning problems, required at least one prompt per problem; compared against a non-AI historical sample (Jansen et al., n=3543) and against ChatGPT's own solo performance (100 runs). Study 2: participants randomized/sampled into AI group (n=245 analyzed, used ChatGPT-4o with same task) vs. no-AI group (n=207 analyzed, no AI assistance), both with monetary incentive for accurate self-assessment.
measures: Task performance (score out of 20 on LSAT logical reasoning items); metacognitive accuracy (difference between estimated and achieved performance, via self-report item "how many...do you think you solved correctly?"); metacognitive sensitivity via trial-level confidence ratings (0-100 slider) and Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis producing Area Under Curve (AUC); AI literacy via the Scale for the Assessment of Non-Experts' AI Literacy (SNAIL, 31 items: Technical Understanding, Critical Appraisal, Practical Application); Dunning-Kruger effect assessed via hierarchical Bayesian computational model estimating latent skill, metacognitive bias (b), and metacognitive noise (sigma); qualitative thematic analysis of chatbot prompts and open-ended question on AI use strategy.
key_finding: Using AI (ChatGPT-4o) improved participants' LSAT performance compared to a no-AI norm sample, but participants overestimated their performance by about four points, showing low metacognitive accuracy; higher AI literacy (SNAIL) was linked to less accurate self-assessment (more confident but less precise). The classic Dunning-Kruger effect (DKE), present in the non-AI comparison sample, "ceased to exist"/disappeared with AI use in both Study 1 and replicated in Study 2, suggesting AI levels metacognitive/cognitive biases across performance levels while simultaneously increasing overall overestimation.
effect_size: Study 1: t(245) = -3.66, p < .001, d = -0.23 (participants vs ChatGPT alone); t(245) = 19.23, p < .001, d = 1.23 (participants+AI vs Jansen et al. no-AI sample); overestimation t(256) = 14.98, p < .001, d = 0.93; confidence correct vs incorrect t(244) = 8.21, p < .001, d = 0.52; AUC vs .5 t(244) = 16.02, p < .001, d = 1.02, mean AUC = .62 (SD=11.2); Q1 vs Q4 difference t(130) = 2.79, p = .006, d = 0.49; DKE model: bias b_AI median = 0.45 (95% HDI [0.32, 0.60]), b_noAI median = 0.23 (95% HDI [0.21, 0.25], p_b=0.0%); noise sigma_noAI median = 1.78 (95% HDI [1.69, 1.88], p_b=0.0%), sigma_AI median = 1.01 (95% HDI [0.84, 1.19], p_b=45.66%). Study 2: AI vs ChatGPT alone t(244) = -2.17, p = .031, d = -0.14; AI vs no-AI t(450) = 12.60, p < .001, d = 1.18; overestimation AI t(244)=18.33, p<.001, d=1.17; no-AI t(206)=11.81, p<.001, d=0.82; bias b_AI median = 0.63 (95% HDI [0.45, 0.85], p_b=0.0%), b_noAI median = 0.75 (95% HDI [0.58, 0.95], p_b=0.0%); sigma_noAI median = 1.53 (95% HDI [1.18, 1.96], p_b=0.1%), sigma_AI median = 1.13 (95% HDI [0.93, 1.36], p_b=10.1%).
limitations: Authors state: the apparent absence of the DKE may not fully reflect underlying cognitive dynamics (AI may have made participants "equally skilled yet unaware" rather than eliminating DKE); reliance on LSAT questions may not capture diversity of real-world reasoning skills/domains and may overlap with AI's training data (though ChatGPT-4o's performance was imperfect at 68.25%, believed findings still apply); focus on LSAT-based reasoning limits scope of metacognitive biases across domains; little effect found of different AI use strategies (tool/collaborator/teammate) on metacognitive accuracy; AI literacy was self-reported, raising challenges similar to DKE itself and self-reported literacy may not translate to effective AI interactions; participants were required to prompt ChatGPT at least once which may not reflect naturalistic usage patterns; study cannot speak to role of metacognition in AI-mediated long-term learning contexts.
caveat_flags: preprint; self-report only (AI literacy, confidence ratings); outcome is proxy not learning; no delayed retention test; quasi-experimental comparison to historical/external no-AI sample (Study 1); not preregistered (not stated); single task domain (LSAT only); unpublished working draft; supplied text capped at 90,000 characters; later sections may be absent; Study 2: random assignment to AI vs no-AI groups not stated in retrieved text (text says the sample was 'split into two groups')

title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Self-Reported Reductions in Cognitive Effort and Confidence Effects From a Survey of Knowledge Workers

n: 319 participants (knowledge workers); 936 real-world task examples analyzed (from 957 collected, after removing 11 low-detail and 11 duplicate/non-GenAI examples); 333 responses …
population: knowledge workers; setting/country not reported in retrieved text; age not reported in retrieved text (described as "knowledge workers", implying adults, but not explicitly stated)
ai_exposure: Generative AI (GenAI) tools used in participants' own work tasks; no controlled arms/conditions, self-reported real-world usage examples

authors: Michael Gerlich
design: mixed-method cross-sectional study combining surveys (ANOVA, correlation analysis) and in-depth interviews (thematic analysis)
n: 666 participants (survey, 'valid' respondents out of 669 recruited); subset of 50 participants for semi-structured interviews; 50 participants used for pilot testing
